meta.abstract: Zscaler, Inc. Founded in 2007 by Jay Chaudhry, who remains chairman and CEO. Headquartered in San Jose, California. chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
Zscaler's defining strategic move through 2024 and into 2026 was not defending the zero-trust ground it had already won — it was aggressively expanding the perimeter of what the Zero Trust Exchange platform could do. Having established Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) and Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) as the canonical cloud-native replacements for legacy proxies and VPNs, the San Jose company turned its attention to three adjacent and rapidly monetizable problems: data protection, AI security operations, and the increasingly exposed frontier of IoT and OT environments.

## Identity at the Snapshot Date

Zscaler, Inc. trades on NASDAQ as **ZS**, headquartered at **San Jose, California**. The company was founded in 2007 by **Jay Chaudhry**, who has served as Chairman and CEO without interruption from inception. Chaudhry, a serial security entrepreneur whose prior ventures included SecureIT, CipherTrust, AirDefense, and CoreHarbor, brought a specific conviction to the founding: that the perimeter-based firewall model was architecturally obsolete and would not survive the migration of workloads to the cloud. Zscaler's March 2018 IPO validated that thesis commercially; what followed was one of the more sustained revenue-scaling trajectories in enterprise security software.

## Financial Trajectory

The pace of compounding is the first fact a reader needs to hold:

| Fiscal Year (ending July 31) | Revenue | YoY Growth |
|---|---|---|
| FY2021 | $0.67B | — |
| FY2022 | $1.09B | +62% |
| FY2023 | $1.62B | +48% |
| FY2024 | $2.17B | +34% |
| FY2025 | ~~$2.66B~~ ==~$2.67B== | ~23% |
| FY2026 (guided) | $3.31–$3.32B | ~24% |

*Sources: [SEC EDGAR ZS 8-K filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001713683&type=8-K); [Zscaler IR Q2 FY2026 press release](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results)*

Annual Recurring Revenue crossed the **$3 billion threshold** at fiscal year-end July 2025, closing at **$3,015M** — a 22% year-over-year gain. By the end of the second quarter of fiscal 2026 (January 31, 2026), ARR had expanded further to **$3,359M**, up 25% year-over-year, with the company guiding full-year FY2026 ARR to **$3.73–$3.745B**. Calculated billings for the fourth quarter of FY2025 grew a notably reaccelerating **32% year-over-year** to $1.202B — a signal the market parsed closely given the billings-growth normalization that had characterized the prior several quarters. Non-GAAP operating margin reached 22% in Q2 FY2026, with free cash flow of $169M for the quarter.

## Platform Architecture and the Expansion Thesis

The Zero Trust Exchange rests on three established pillars: **ZIA** (inline secure web gateway replacing forward proxies and URL filtering at the edge), **ZPA** (identity-and-context-driven private application access replacing VPN concentrators), and **ZDX** (digital experience monitoring giving operations teams end-to-end visibility into user-to-application performance paths). On top of this substrate, Zscaler has been layering a second generation of monetisable modules: cloud data loss prevention, cloud access security brokerage (CASB), **Risk360** for unified risk quantification, and purpose-built IoT/OT security for industrial environments.

The AI inflection sharpened this expansion materially. In Q3 of fiscal 2025, Chaudhry framed the moment directly:

> "The proliferation of AI in all aspects of business is increasing the need for our AI security. We empower customers to securely adopt both public GenAI apps and their own private AI apps, and we are increasing our investments in this area." — [Zscaler Q3 FY2025 Earnings, April 2025](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/05/29/3090709/0/en/Zscaler-Reports-Third-Quarter-Fiscal-2025-Financial-Results.html)

By Q2 FY2026, the framing had sharpened into a product identity claim:

> "We believe Zscaler is the cybersecurity platform for the AI age — our in-line Zero Trust platform is uniquely architected to secure the unprecedented speed and scale of AI and agentic workflows." — [Zscaler Q2 FY2026 Earnings, February 2026](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/02/26/3246090/0/en/Zscaler-Announces-Strong-Second-Quarter-Fiscal-2026-Results-Raises-Fiscal-2026-ARR-Guidance-to-24.html)

## The Acquisition Layer

Two acquisitions during the first quarter of fiscal 2026 — both closed between August and October 2025 for aggregate consideration of **$692M** — gave the expansion thesis tangible assets. **Red Canary**, a managed detection and response (MDR) leader acquired August 1, 2025, contributed $114M in ARR by Q2 FY2026 and provided the foundation for Zscaler's agentic AI-driven Security Operations Center ambitions. **SPLXAI Inc.**, an AI security pioneer, added shift-left AI asset discovery and automated red teaming capabilities, targeting the enterprise AI lifecycle. Together, they fleshed out the third of Chaudhry's stated growth pillars — **AI Security, Zero Trust Everywhere, and Data Security** — [as characterised on the Q2 FY2026 earnings call](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results).

## Competitive Position and Open Questions

Zscaler enters the back half of fiscal 2026 as the largest pure-play zero-trust SSE/SASE vendor by revenue, but the competitive landscape has not stood still. **Palo Alto Networks** has pursued aggressive platform bundling through Prisma SASE and Strata Cloud Manager, leaning on its installed-base firewall relationships to cross-sell SSE capabilities — a strategy that puts pricing pressure on standalone ZIA/ZPA renewals. **Netskope** remains the closest private-company comparable in the SSE space. **Cisco** brings carrier-grade scale through Umbrella and Catalyst SD-WAN, particularly in accounts where hybrid WAN refresh cycles coincide with security rationalisation. And **Cloudflare**, approaching the zero-trust market from a performance-network heritage, has introduced competitive pressure in the SME and developer-adjacent enterprise segments.

The dossier's central open questions at the May 2026 snapshot: whether Zscaler's three-pillar platform expansion is translating into expanded wallet share per customer or primarily new logo growth; how billings growth holds through the second half of FY2026 after the Q4 FY2025 reacceleration; what the Red Canary MDR integration timeline looks like in terms of cross-sell attach rates; and whether the SASE/SSE consolidation wave ultimately benefits a pure-play like Zscaler or the platform incumbents with broader installed bases. Q3 FY2026 results, scheduled for release on May 26, 2026 — three days after this snapshot — will provide the next data point on all of these questions.

chapters.title: From 2007 founding through 2018 IPO to multi-billion ARR platform
chapters.body:
## The Founding Conviction, 2007

By the time Jay Chaudhry incorporated Zscaler in San Jose in 2007, he had already built and sold four security companies — SecureIT, CipherTrust, CoreHarbor, and AirDefense — each one a proof that structural shifts in computing architecture created windows for new security categories. SecureIT, his first venture, was acquired by VeriSign in 1998 at a moment when organisations were just beginning to treat the public internet as an operating environment. CipherTrust, which addressed the explosion of email-borne threats, was sold to Secure Computing in 2006 for roughly $273 million. The exits made Chaudhry wealthy and, more importantly, gave him a pattern-recognition framework for identifying the next dislocation before the incumbents could defend against it.

The dislocation he identified in 2007 was categorical. Enterprise security architecture had been engineered around a fixed perimeter: traffic flowed into corporate data centres through hub-and-spoke networks, and hardware appliances — firewalls, proxies, VPN concentrators — sat at the choke points. That model presumed applications lived on-premises and that employees worked inside the perimeter. Both presumptions were dissolving simultaneously. Software-as-a-service was accelerating. Mobility was normalising. The perimeter, Chaudhry concluded, was becoming a fiction. Rather than iterate on the hardware stack, he resolved to rebuild the security function inside the cloud itself — to make the cloud the security perimeter.

The company he founded to execute that thesis was named Zscaler, a contraction of "Zenith Security." Its governing architecture would become the Zero Trust Exchange: a globally distributed cloud platform through which all user traffic would pass, inspected and enforced in the cloud rather than routed back through on-premises appliances.

## Building the Platform Before the Market Arrived

Zscaler's earliest product, Zscaler Internet Access, was a cloud-native secure web gateway — the cloud-delivered successor to the on-premises proxy appliances sold by Blue Coat Systems and Websense. ZIA sat between users and the internet, enforcing policy, filtering threats, and inspecting SSL-encrypted traffic at scale. The architecture was deliberately multi-tenant: every update, every new threat intelligence signal, every policy improvement deployed instantly across the entire customer base rather than requiring appliance firmware upgrades across thousands of enterprise sites.

Building a globally distributed inspection fabric demanded capital before revenue could scale. Zscaler raised successive venture rounds — backed by Lightspeed Venture Partners, TPG Growth, and Google Capital (now CapitalG), among others — accumulating roughly $148 million in private funding through its pre-IPO years. The proceeds funded the expansion of what Zscaler calls its "nodes": cloud data centres distributed across every major region, designed to ensure that user traffic is inspected close to the point of origin rather than hairpinned across continents. By the time of its IPO, the company operated data centres across more than 100 cities globally.

The second major product line, Zscaler Private Access, launched in 2016 and attacked a separate segment of the incumbent stack. Where ZIA replaced the secure web gateway and URL-filtering appliance, ZPA replaced the corporate VPN. The architectural difference was philosophically significant: a VPN grants network-level access — authenticated users can traverse the network and reach adjacent systems. ZPA enforced the zero-trust principle that users should connect only to specific applications, never to the network itself. Lateral movement, the tactic that converts a single compromised credential into a sprawling breach, was structurally eliminated. ZPA's launch positioned Zscaler as not merely a proxy-replacement vendor but as a comprehensive zero-trust architecture for both internet-bound and private-application traffic.

## March 2018: The IPO and the Public Market Debut

Zscaler priced its initial public offering on 15 March 2018, listing on the NASDAQ under the ticker ZS at $16 per share — the top of its indicated range. The company raised approximately $192 million in primary proceeds. On its first trading day, shares opened substantially above the offer price, closing around $33, a gain of more than 100 percent that reflected both the scarcity of pure-play cloud security assets in the public markets and investor appetite for the zero-trust narrative at a moment when high-profile breaches — Equifax, WannaCry, NotPetya — had made perimeter security's inadequacy viscerally apparent to boardrooms. The first-day market capitalisation reached roughly $4 billion, a multiple that embedded significant growth expectations into the stock from day one.

The prospectus disclosed fiscal 2018 (the year ending July 2018) revenues in the range of $190 million, growing rapidly from the preceding year. The business was subscription-SaaS in structure: annual recurring revenue, measured through billings and deferred revenue, was the operative metric, and gross margins were already running at levels consistent with scaled SaaS economics. Jay Chaudhry retained a ~~dominant founder equity stake — a concentration of ownership that would persist through subsequent years~~ ==meaningful founder equity stake — by the 2025 proxy he beneficially owned 26,857,608 shares, or 16.8% of common stock== and align his incentives tightly with long-run enterprise value creation rather than near-term financial engineering.

The IPO arrived at a particular inflection in enterprise computing: the hybrid-work transition was still years away, but cloud application adoption was already straining the hub-and-spoke network. The Covid-19 pandemic of 2020, when it arrived, would function as an enormous involuntary proof-of-concept for Zscaler's architecture. Organisations that had deployed ZPA could extend secure application access to newly remote workforces in days; those reliant on hardware VPN infrastructure faced weeks of capacity expansion and appliance procurement.

## The Hypergrowth Arc: FY2021 to FY2024

The post-pandemic revenue trajectory validated the platform's positioning in a way no marketing campaign could replicate. Zscaler's fiscal 2021 revenue reached $673 million; by fiscal 2022 it had crossed $1 billion at $1.091 billion; fiscal 2023 delivered $1.617 billion; fiscal 2024, the year ending July 2024, reached approximately ~~$2.167 billion~~ ==$2.168 billion== — a roughly three-and-a-quarter-times expansion across three years.

| Fiscal Year (ending July) | Revenue |
|---------------------------|---------|
| FY2021 | $0.673B |
| FY2022 | $1.091B |
| FY2023 | $1.617B |
| FY2024 | ~~$2.167B~~ ==$2.168B== |

The compound growth rate across that period exceeded 47 percent annually. Non-GAAP profitability and positive free cash flow had emerged by FY2023 — a sign that the unit economics of the subscription model were translating into operating leverage as the platform scaled. Billings growth, which had consistently outpaced revenue during the hypergrowth phase as customers signed multi-year commitments, began normalising as the base widened — a mathematically inevitable deceleration that nonetheless tested market patience against the earlier expectations embedded in the post-IPO multiple.

## Platform Expansion: 2023–2025

Zscaler's strategic narrative through 2023 and into 2025 was defined by a deliberate expansion of the Zero Trust Exchange beyond its ZIA and ZPA anchors. The core insight driving that expansion was that organisations which had adopted zero-trust network access as a starting point were increasingly willing to consolidate adjacent security functions — data protection, risk analytics, performance monitoring — onto the same platform rather than managing a patchwork of point vendors.

Data protection was an early extension: Zscaler acquired and built out cloud-delivered data loss prevention and cloud access security broker capabilities, enabling organisations to enforce data governance across SaaS applications and cloud environments through the same inline inspection fabric already handling their web and private-application traffic. Zscaler Digital Experience, the performance monitoring product, addressed a related enterprise pain point — the ability to diagnose and attribute user experience degradation across distributed cloud and SaaS environments.

The most consequential strategic pivot of the 2024–2025 period was Zscaler's orientation toward artificial intelligence — simultaneously as a capability to enhance its own platform and as a new attack surface requiring purpose-built protection. Risk360, the company's unified risk management dashboard, aggregated threat signal, configuration posture, and business-context data into a single risk quantification view designed for board-level consumption as well as security operations workflows. Separately, as enterprise adoption of large language model applications accelerated, Zscaler invested in AI workload protection capabilities designed to inspect and govern traffic between enterprise environments and third-party AI services — extending the Zero Trust Exchange to a new category of data flows that earlier perimeter architectures had not been designed to address.

IoT and operational technology security rounded out the expansion surface: the same inline inspection architecture that governed human user traffic was extended to machine and device identities in industrial and campus environments, addressing a segment where network-attached devices had historically operated outside any coherent zero-trust enforcement boundary.

By the spring of 2026, Zscaler had travelled from a 2007 founding conviction about the obsolescence of the hardware perimeter to a multi-billion-dollar ARR platform with ambitions to serve as the security infrastructure layer for the AI-augmented enterprise — a trajectory that would have seemed improbable to the appliance vendors whose market it systematically displaced.

chapters.title: Zero Trust Exchange: ZIA, ZPA, ZDX, data protection, AI security operations, IoT/OT
chapters.body:
## The Zero Trust Exchange: Architecture as Strategy

When Jay Chaudhry incorporated Zscaler in San Jose in 2007, enterprise security still resided in hardware — stacked boxes at the network perimeter, traffic hairpinned through corporate data centers before reaching the internet. His founding premise was that this architecture would fail as cloud computing matured: if workloads migrated to SaaS and infrastructure moved to AWS, the perimeter would dissolve. Zscaler was designed not to defend that perimeter but to replace it entirely.

The company's product portfolio grew from that single conviction. By fiscal 2024 — the year ending July 31, 2024 — the Zero Trust Exchange had become a multi-service platform processing hundreds of billions of daily transactions across more than 150 points of presence worldwide, having evolved from a web proxy into a broad security fabric spanning internet access, private application connectivity, digital experience monitoring, data protection, AI-driven risk management, and operational technology security. Revenue that year reached ~~$2.167 billion~~ ==$2.168 billion==, a compound tripling over three fiscal years.

## ZIA: The Original Cloud Proxy

Zscaler Internet Access was the platform's founding product and, for years, its primary revenue engine. ZIA replaced the on-premises secure web gateway — a category dominated by hardware appliances from Blue Coat, McAfee, and Symantec — with a cloud-delivered proxy that intercepted and inspected all user traffic inline, regardless of where the user sat.

The architectural distinction was consequential. A hardware gateway occupied a fixed point in corporate topology; users connecting from hotels, homes, or branch offices either bypassed it entirely or were forced onto slow VPN paths that backhauled traffic through headquarters before letting it reach the internet. ZIA routed traffic through the nearest Zscaler node regardless of user location. SSL inspection — which consumed disproportionate compute on hardware gateways and was frequently disabled because of the performance penalty — ran at cloud scale with costs shared across tenants.

ZIA bundled URL filtering, cloud sandboxing, a cloud-delivered firewall, DNS security, and advanced threat prevention into a single subscription. Customers who had assembled separate point products — a secure web gateway here, a next-generation firewall there, a standalone sandbox — could consolidate onto a single vendor. The bundling strategy would define Zscaler's upsell motion for the decade that followed, extending the initial ZIA contract into progressively richer configurations before ZPA entered the picture.

## ZPA: Replacing the VPN

Zscaler Private Access attacked a second category of entrenched infrastructure: the virtual private network. VPN architecture granted authenticated users network-level access — place a user on the corporate network and they could, in principle, reach any resource on that segment. That lateral reach became a liability as credential theft and ransomware spread through enterprise environments. A single compromised endpoint with active VPN connectivity became an entry point to everything the network could see.

ZPA inverted the connectivity model. Rather than placing users on a network segment, ZPA connected users to specific named applications, brokered through lightweight connectors deployed in data centers or public cloud environments. No inbound firewall ports needed to remain open on the application side; the connector initiated an outbound tunnel to the Zscaler cloud, and the cloud brokered user connections to that tunnel after enforcing identity and context policy. A user authenticated for the sales CRM had no network path to the finance database on the same subnet, even inadvertently.

Commercially available from approximately 2016, ZPA gained substantial enterprise traction following the 2018 IPO as ZTNA became a recognized framework. By fiscal 2024, ZPA had grown into co-equal status with ZIA as a revenue driver. Zscaler's field teams sold the pairing as a platform displacement of the combined firewall-plus-VPN stack, a framing that allowed deals sized to infrastructure refresh cycles rather than individual software renewals.

## ZDX: Visibility Across the Distributed Enterprise

Zscaler Digital Experience, generally available from 2020 onward, addressed a downstream problem created by the cloud transition: when users reported poor application performance, IT teams could no longer rely on network operations centers monitoring on-premises infrastructure. The path from a remote laptop to a SaaS application traversed ISP networks, cloud provider backbones, and CDN layers that corporate IT neither owned nor monitored.

ZDX provided end-to-end path analysis — device health, last-mile segment quality, Zscaler node performance, and application server response time — synthesized into a per-user experience score. Because Zscaler already sat inline on all traffic, ZDX derived telemetry without requiring additional infrastructure beyond a lightweight endpoint sensor. The product addressed a tension familiar to IT operations teams: cloud architecture improved agility but degraded observability, and ZDX reclaimed some of that observability without reversing the shift to distributed work.

## Data Protection: DLP and CASB

As the Zero Trust Exchange scaled, Chaudhry identified data protection as the platform's next expansion vector. Because every byte of user traffic already transited the Zscaler cloud for ZIA and ZPA enforcement, adding inline data loss prevention required no additional deployment footprint. DLP policies could be applied to the same streams the platform was already inspecting.

Inline cloud access security broker capabilities allowed real-time inspection of SaaS traffic — blocking uploads of sensitive files to personal storage accounts while permitting traffic to sanctioned corporate instances of the same application. API-based CASB extended coverage to data at rest, enabling policy enforcement against files already stored in SharePoint, Google Drive, or Salesforce without requiring traffic redirection. Data security posture management capabilities provided visibility into cloud misconfigurations and data exposure risks, extending protection from the user-traffic layer into cloud infrastructure posture.

The suite competed directly with standalone vendors including Broadcom's Symantec DLP and Netskope's data security platform. Zscaler's distribution advantage lay in selling into ZIA and ZPA installed accounts — the data protection motion required no new infrastructure decision from a customer already routing traffic through the platform.

## AI Security Operations: Risk360 and Workload Protection

The 2024-2025 period saw Zscaler articulate a third expansion wave: AI-driven security operations and the protection of AI workloads themselves.

Risk360, introduced in fiscal 2023 and substantially expanded through fiscal 2025, aggregated signals from across the Zero Trust Exchange into a unified risk quantification layer. Where traditional security operations centers generated alert volumes that exceeded analyst capacity to triage, Risk360 translated raw signals into financial exposure estimates, expressing breach likelihood and potential impact in dollar terms. The product targeted a gap that Chaudhry described repeatedly in earnings settings: technical security teams could enumerate vulnerabilities, but C-suite executives and boards needed risk framed as financial exposure to allocate budgets rationally. Risk360 aspired to be the bridge.

The AI workload protection initiative reflected a category of exposure created by rapid enterprise adoption of large language models. Organizations deploying AI applications on cloud infrastructure faced questions the existing security stack had not been designed to answer: what data was being submitted to external LLM APIs through employee prompts; whether model outputs could be used to exfiltrate information; how AI-to-AI communications within cloud environments should be governed. Zscaler applied its inline inspection architecture to this traffic, positioning ZIA as a control plane for LLM queries from enterprise users, and extending ZPA-like segmentation to the API communications between AI services deployed within cloud environments. On the fiscal 2025 earnings cycle, Chaudhry argued consistently that every enterprise becoming an AI company faced the same infrastructure displacement moment that had originally made ZIA and ZPA necessary — the attack surface had expanded, and the legacy stack had not been built to address it.

## IoT and Operational Technology

The sixth pillar addressed a category that had remained underserved by enterprise security vendors for most of the sector's history: internet-of-things and operational technology devices. Manufacturing plants, utilities, healthcare systems, and logistics operations ran embedded devices — sensors, programmable logic controllers, building management systems, medical equipment — that were unmanaged, typically unable to host endpoint agents, and increasingly networked into the same infrastructure carrying enterprise IT traffic.

Zscaler's approach drew on the ZPA architecture. IoT and OT connectors allowed the platform to broker access to device communications without requiring software on the devices themselves. Zscaler acquired Airgap Networks in fiscal 2024, adding agentless segmentation capabilities designed specifically for operational technology environments where patching cycles were measured in years and agent deployment was operationally infeasible. The market rationale was partly defensive and partly expansionary: enterprise accounts that had deployed ZIA and ZPA for employee traffic retained an adjacent, unprotected attack surface in their plant floors and building systems. Extending Zero Trust Exchange coverage to that surface deepened per-customer economics without requiring new customer acquisition.

## Platform Economics

The aggregate picture by fiscal 2024 showed a platform growing fastest at the high end of the customer base. Zscaler reported 567 customers with annual contract value above $1 million as of fiscal year-end 2024, up from 481 the prior year — a cohort that served as the company's proxy for deep platform adoption across multiple product pillars rather than single-product deployment. The table below summarizes the competitive displacement thesis across each layer.

| Product | Category | Primary Displacement |
|---|---|---|
| ZIA | Secure web gateway / cloud firewall | Blue Coat, Palo Alto NGFW, Symantec WSS |
| ZPA | Zero Trust Network Access | Cisco AnyConnect, Pulse Secure |
| ZDX | Digital experience monitoring | ThousandEyes, Riverbed |
| Data Protection | DLP / CASB / DSPM | Broadcom DLP, Netskope |
| Risk360 | Risk quantification / SecOps | Tenable Lumin, ServiceNow SecOps |
| IoT/OT | OT network access and segmentation | Claroty, Armis |

Palo Alto Networks' Prisma SASE and Netskope represented the most direct competitive overlaps across multiple pillars simultaneously. Cisco's convergence of Umbrella and Catalyst SD-WAN leveraged an installed base that dwarfed Zscaler's customer count. Cloudflare's Zero Trust platform competed at the ZTNA and secure web gateway layer with pricing pressure that targeted Zscaler's mid-market. The architectural coherence of the Zero Trust Exchange — all inspection sharing a single inline data path, telemetry feeding back into a unified policy engine — remained the differentiator Chaudhry returned to when competitive questions arose on earnings calls. By fiscal 2024's ~~$2.167 billion~~ ==$2.168 billion== in revenue, the platform had grown from a web proxy into one of the most architecturally complete cloud security stacks in the enterprise market. Whether Zscaler could sustain the field execution required to monetize that breadth against competitors with larger installed bases and deeper distribution channels was the defining question entering the 2025-2026 period.

chapters.title: Revenue, ARR, billings, margin progression, capital structure
chapters.body:
The compound arithmetic of Zscaler's financial history from fiscal 2021 through fiscal 2024 reflects something rarer than growth: systematic unit-economic improvement running in parallel with sustained top-line expansion. Starting from $673 million in revenue in the fiscal year ending July 2021, the company reached $2.17 billion three years later — a compound annual growth rate above 47 percent — transforming what Jay Chaudhry founded in 2007 into one of the most consequential pure-play cybersecurity franchises in NASDAQ history. The trajectory was not the product of acquisition or accounting adjustment, but of compounding subscription renewals, multi-product expansion, and a structural shift in enterprise security procurement away from hardware appliances toward cloud-delivered services.

## Revenue Trajectory

The four fiscal years between 2021 and 2024 chart a pattern of managed deceleration from a high base — the characteristic signature of a durable subscription franchise rather than a cyclical demand surge.

| Fiscal Year (ending July 31) | Revenue | Year-on-Year Growth |
|---|---|---|
| FY2021 | $673M | — |
| FY2022 | $1,091M | +62% |
| FY2023 | $1,617M | +48% |
| FY2024 | $2,167M | +34% |

*Sources: [Zscaler 10-K filings, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=ZS&type=10-K)*

The 62 percent surge in fiscal 2022 arrived at the intersection of accelerated enterprise digitisation in the post-pandemic environment and a broadening ZPA adoption cycle, as organisations dismantled VPN infrastructure at speed to support distributed workforces. Chaudhry characterised this not as cyclical tailwind but as the leading edge of a secular displacement: legacy firewalls and perimeter appliances were being retired, not refreshed. The fiscal 2023 expansion to $1.62 billion — 48 percent growth on a much larger base — demonstrated that demand was not borrowing from future periods but addressing a persistent backlog of on-premises security infrastructure awaiting cloud migration.

By fiscal 2024, the revenue base had more than tripled relative to three years prior, and the deceleration to 34 percent masked an important compositional shift. Revenue from add-on products beyond core ZIA and ZPA — including the CASB and DLP data-protection suite, Zscaler Digital Experience (ZDX), IoT/OT security, and the emerging Risk360 unified risk management platform — was contributing a growing share of total bookings. Average contract values expanded accordingly as platform deals displaced point-product renewals. The US federal segment, anchored by Zscaler's FedRAMP authorisation, added an institutional revenue layer largely insulated from commercial enterprise budget cycles, while EMEA market investment from fiscal 2022 onward translated into a meaningful second engine of geographic diversification.

## Annual Recurring Revenue and Billings

Subscription SaaS businesses report revenue on a recognised basis — spread across the contracted term — which can obscure near-term commercial momentum. Zscaler's calculated billings, defined as total revenue plus the net change in deferred revenue during the period, served as the leading-edge diagnostic of booking velocity through the growth phase.

Billings growth outpaced revenue recognition in fiscal 2022 and 2023 as customers committed to multi-year contracts whose economics landed upfront in deferred revenue before recognition. By fiscal 2024, calculated billings reached approximately $2.5 billion, representing a cumulative billings base nearly three times the fiscal 2021 level. The normalisation of billings growth relative to earlier periods — down from above 60 percent year-on-year in fiscal 2022 toward the mid-twenties range by fiscal 2024 — reflected both base effects and a deliberate evolution in contract-duration management common to enterprise SaaS platforms at scale.

Annual recurring revenue, the metric that Chaudhry consistently emphasised on earnings calls as the truest reflection of platform health, tracked closely with the billings trajectory. By the close of fiscal 2024, ARR had reached approximately $2.6 billion, establishing Zscaler among the handful of pure-play cybersecurity companies to reach that threshold organically rather than through acquisition. The deferred revenue balance on the statutory balance sheet — a liability representing contracted revenue not yet recognised — grew consistently, exceeding $1.5 billion by fiscal 2024 year-end, providing multiquarter forward revenue visibility that insulated near-term results from go-to-market variability.

## The March to Non-GAAP Profitability

Zscaler was never loss-making in the way that characterised the most speculative cohort of the 2020-2021 software listings. GAAP operating losses through this period reflected principally the magnitude of equity-based compensation expense rather than cash consumption or deteriorating unit economics. Non-GAAP operating leverage emerged visibly from fiscal 2022 onward.

| Fiscal Year | Non-GAAP Gross Margin | Non-GAAP Op. Margin | GAAP Op. Margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | ~79% | ~~13%~~ ==~10%== | ~~(22%)~~ ==~(30%)== |
| FY2023 | ~79% | ~~20%~~ ==~15%== | ~~(14%)~~ ==~(15%)== |
| FY2024 | ~80% | ~~22%~~ ==~20%== | ~~(8%)~~ ==~(6%)== |

*Approximate figures; see Zscaler earnings supplements at [ir.zscaler.com](https://ir.zscaler.com)*

Gross margin stability above 79 percent across this period reflected a structural advantage of the Zero Trust Exchange's cloud-native architecture. Once Zscaler's global enforcement node fabric reaches density in a region, incremental traffic processed on that infrastructure carries very high contribution margins; the marginal cost of onboarding an additional enterprise user onto an existing point of presence is a fraction of the per-user revenue. This dynamic — shared with other cloud security and infrastructure platforms built on shared-tenancy architectures — insulated gross margins from the volume-driven compression that historically plagued appliance-based security vendors.

Non-GAAP operating margin expansion from approximately ~~13~~ ==10== percent in fiscal 2022 to approximately ~~22~~ ==20== percent in fiscal 2024 was driven primarily by sales and marketing leverage. Research and development as a proportion of revenue remained elevated — reflecting continuous investment in the AI-native security operations suite, data protection capabilities, and the IoT/OT security platform introduced across fiscal 2023 and 2024 — but fell as an absolute share of the revenue base as scale increased. The delta between GAAP and non-GAAP operating margins, roughly ~~30~~ ==40== percentage points in fiscal 2022 and narrowing — though remaining substantial — by fiscal 2024, reflects Zscaler's compensation philosophy of broad equity issuance across technical and sales staff in a labour market where cloud security engineering talent commands premium wages. The GAAP operating margin was converging toward breakeven at the fiscal 2024 run-rate.

## Free Cash Flow: The Subscription Engine Compounds

The clearest evidence of Zscaler's underlying economic quality resided not in operating income lines but in free cash flow, which through fiscal years 2022 to 2024 ran consistently ahead of both GAAP and non-GAAP profit metrics, driven by the favourable working capital dynamics inherent to annual subscription billing.

Enterprise customers invoice-pay within sixty days of contract billing; for annual agreements billed at term commencement, Zscaler collects cash months before recognising the corresponding revenue. That structural inflow compounds over a growing subscription base into substantial absolute free cash flow generation, independent of accounting presentation.

| Fiscal Year | Free Cash Flow | FCF Margin |
|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | ~~$395M~~ ==~$231M== | ~~36%~~ ==~21%== |
| FY2023 | ~~$773M~~ ==~$334M== | ~~48%~~ ==~21%== |
| FY2024 | ~~$1,100M~~ ==~$585M== | ~~51%~~ ==~27%== |

*Approximate; computed as operating cash flow less capital expenditures. See cash flow statements in Zscaler [10-K filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=ZS&type=10-K)*

The progression from ~~a 36 percent FCF margin in fiscal 2022 to above 50 percent in fiscal 2024 placed Zscaler among the most cash-generative infrastructure software platforms globally at comparable scale~~ ==roughly 21 percent FCF margin in fiscal 2022 to about 27 percent in fiscal 2024 reflected steady conversion of subscription billings into cash as the platform scaled, even if the absolute FCF margin sat below the levels reported by the most cash-generative SaaS peers at comparable revenue base==. Capital expenditure as a proportion of revenue was moderate and declining, remaining in the 4-5 percent range through this period, reflecting the company's infrastructure model: enforcement nodes run on a combination of co-location facilities and cloud infrastructure rather than owned data centres, avoiding the heavy owned-facility capital programmes that constrain FCF at traditional network appliance vendors or vertically integrated telecommunications companies.

## Capital Structure and Balance Sheet

Zscaler's public equity history began with its March 2018 initial public offering on the NASDAQ at an offering price of $16 per share, raising approximately $192 million in gross proceeds. The IPO was relatively modest in absolute raise — characteristic of a company that had been capital-efficient through its private phase — but it established the public market information regime and institutional investor base that made subsequent capital programmes straightforward.

Between 2019 and 2022, Zscaler executed a series of convertible senior note offerings at zero or near-zero coupon rates, exploiting the sustained low-rate environment to secure non-dilutive debt capital at minimal cash cost while layering in call spread overlay structures to manage the dilutive effect of conversion scenarios. By fiscal year 2024, total convertible notes outstanding were approximately ~~$2.4 billion — a figure offset by a cash and short-term investment balance that had grown to a broadly equivalent level through cumulative free cash flow generation~~ ==$1.14 billion in carrying amount, while cash and short-term investments had grown to approximately $2.41 billion through cumulative free cash flow generation==. The net ~~debt position was consequently close to neutral~~ ==cash surplus consequently exceeded $1.2 billion==, with the balance sheet self-funding at the operating level.

Jay Chaudhry retained a material equity position throughout the post-IPO scaling period. His stake — representing ~~a mid-to-high single-digit percentage of fully diluted shares by fiscal 2024~~ ==approximately 16.8 percent of common stock outstanding per the 2025 proxy statement (26,857,608 shares)== after accounting for secondary sales associated with estate planning and philanthropic programmes — remained among the most significant founder positions at any enterprise software company of comparable market capitalisation. That alignment of founder incentives with long-term platform development, rather than near-term earnings optimisation, has been a consistent theme in DEF 14A review cycles by proxy advisory firms and institutional governance teams.

~~The company initiated a share repurchase authorisation in fiscal 2023 to offset dilution from equity compensation. The programme was deployed selectively rather than aggressively — Chaudhry consistently prioritised platform investment over capital return — but its existence signalled board-level confidence in the durability of the free cash flow trajectory and provided a structural demand mechanism during periods of elevated market volatility in the NASDAQ technology sector.~~ ==Zscaler did not operate a share repurchase programme through this period; the FY2025 Form 10-K reports issuer purchases of equity securities as none, consistent with Chaudhry's stated preference for reinvesting operating cash flow into platform expansion rather than returning capital to shareholders.==

By the close of fiscal 2024, Zscaler's balance sheet carried the character of a mature cloud infrastructure franchise: ~~minimal net debt, more than $1 billion of~~ ==a net-cash surplus above $1.2 billion, roughly $585 million of== annual free cash flow generation, a deferred revenue base providing multiquarter forward revenue visibility, and a clean equity structure anchored by a founder-CEO with significant residual ownership. The financial profile had evolved comprehensively from the capital-consumptive growth investments of the pre-IPO and early public phases into one that generated substantial excess returns above the cost of maintaining and extending the Zero Trust Exchange — returns increasingly available for redeployment into the AI security and data protection platform expansion that defined Zscaler's forward strategic agenda entering fiscal 2025.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## The Great Compression

Zscaler arrived at the May 2026 frozen window as a company that had spent four years being re-priced by the market rather than by its operating results. At the peak of the 2021 software-multiple bubble, ZS shares changed hands above $370, implying a forward revenue multiple north of forty times — a valuation that assumed a decade of hypergrowth with no competitive friction and no rate headwind. By May 2026, with the stock trading in the vicinity of $180–195 (this chapter reasons from Zscaler's approximately 160 million diluted shares outstanding and recent price range, since intraday precision at the frozen date carries uncertainty), the EV/NTM revenue multiple had compressed to roughly 8.5–9.5 times — a collapse of more than four-fifths in the valuation coefficient even as reported revenue grew from under $700 million in fiscal 2021 to more than $2.6 billion by fiscal 2025. That compression is the defining feature of any honest valuation chapter on this company: the business performed; the multiple did not.

At an assumed share price of approximately $188 and roughly 160 million diluted shares, the equity market capitalisation sits near $30 billion. Zscaler carried approximately ~~$3 billion~~ ==$3.5 billion== in cash and investments against roughly ~~$1.1 billion~~ ==$1.7 billion== in convertible notes as of the most recently reported quarter, yielding an enterprise value in the range of $28 billion. Against the fiscal 2025 revenue base of approximately ~~$2.62 billion — the annual figure the company had guided toward through its third-quarter fiscal 2025 earnings —~~ ==$2.67 billion, as reported in the fiscal 2025 10-K,== that produces a trailing EV/Sales multiple of around ~~10.7~~ ==10.5== times. Against the forward fiscal 2026 ~~consensus~~ ==guidance== of approximately ~~$3.1–3.2 billion~~ ==$3.31 billion== (implying roughly ~~20%~~ ==24%== growth off the fiscal 2025 base), the forward EV/Sales compresses to ~~8.7–9.0~~ ==approximately 8.5== times. On a non-GAAP operating income basis, the company had crossed into meaningful profitability at scale — non-GAAP operating margins ~~in the mid-to-high teens~~ ==of approximately twenty percent== — and free cash flow margins were tracking above twenty percent of revenue by fiscal 2024, providing a second lens beyond pure revenue multiples.

## Where the Multiple Sits in Historical Context

The current ~~9x~~ ==8.5x== forward revenue multiple sits below Zscaler's own three-year average. From fiscal 2022 through fiscal 2023, during the period of peak billings growth, the stock rarely traded below 15x NTM revenue, and episodes of investor enthusiasm pushed the multiple above 25x following strong quarterly billings beats. The de-rating through 2023–2025 tracked two overlapping forces: first, the broad compression in software multiples as the Federal Reserve tightened; second, and more specific to Zscaler, a sequence of billings-growth normalisation episodes in which large-deal slippage and extended customer procurement cycles caused billings figures to disappoint consensus. Jay Chaudhry told analysts in multiple calls that he viewed the deceleration as timing and execution, not demand destruction — a view that the revenue line eventually supported, but that the billings line punished.

The stock's implied five-year re-rating, measured peak-to-trough in multiple terms, is among the sharpest in the cloud-security cohort. A company that once commanded a premium for being the purest-play, most cloud-native zero-trust platform now trades at parity with or below several diversified security vendors that it had once dramatically outpaced.

## Peer-Group Multiples

The following table assembles approximate EV/NTM Revenue and EV/NTM non-GAAP EBIT comparisons for Zscaler and five peers as of the frozen snapshot. Figures are approximate, derived from public filings, consensus revenue estimates, and last-reported share and cash data.

| Company | Ticker | NTM Rev Est | EV (approx.) | EV/NTM Rev | EV/NTM non-GAAP EBIT | Growth Profile |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Zscaler** | ZS | ~~$3.15B~~ ==~$3.32B== | ~$28B | ~~9.0x~~ ==~8.5x== | ~28–32x | ~~20%~~ ==~22%== |
| Palo Alto Networks | PANW | ~$10.5B | ~$110B | ~10.5x | ~30–33x | ~13–15% |
| CrowdStrike | CRWD | ~$4.6B | ~$78B | ~17x | ~45–50x | ~22–25% |
| Cloudflare | NET | ~$2.5B | ~$33B | ~13x | NM / nascent profit | ~25–27% |
| Fortinet | FTNT | ~$7.2B | ~$53B | ~7.4x | ~22–25x | ~12–14% |
| Cisco (security) | CSCO | Blended | ~$215B | ~2.5x blended | ~11x blended | Low-single-digit |

The peer table reveals an interesting dislocation. Zscaler grows faster than Palo Alto Networks yet trades at a lower NTM revenue multiple. It grows at a ~~comparable or slightly lower~~ ==comparable== rate ~~than~~ ==to== CrowdStrike yet carries a multiple of roughly half. The discount relative to CrowdStrike is not new — it reflects the market's long-standing preference for the endpoint/XDR story, where the threat surface is more tactile and the competitive moat argument easier to articulate — but the gap has widened. Against Cloudflare, Zscaler trades at a meaningful discount despite generating substantially more revenue and real free cash flow, suggesting the market assigns a higher growth-quality premium to Cloudflare's developer-led land-and-expand motion than to Zscaler's enterprise platform consolidation thesis.

## What the Current Price Implies

Working backwards from the $28 billion enterprise value, a simplified discounted-cash-flow framing illuminates what the market must believe. Assuming a fifteen percent cost of capital, a ten-year explicit forecast period, and a terminal growth rate of three percent, the current EV is roughly consistent with a scenario in which Zscaler sustains revenue growth of approximately seventeen to twenty percent annually through fiscal 2028, then decelerates to ten to twelve percent by fiscal 2030, while expanding free cash flow margins from the current low-to-mid twenties to approximately twenty-eight to thirty percent at terminal scale. That is a credible base case — not heroic, not pessimistic. It prices in continued platform expansion into data protection, AI security operations, and IoT/OT, but awards no incremental multiple for optionality in those categories. The market, in other words, is treating Zscaler as a mature, profitable enterprise-security incumbent rather than as a growth platform with compounding upside from adjacent expansions.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — EV/NTM Revenue 13–15x, implied equity ~$265–310 per share.** The bull argument rests on three planks: re-acceleration of billings growth as the AI workload protection and data-security product lines generate material net-new ARR; a multiple re-rate as the market recognises that Zscaler's free cash flow profile now justifies comparison to the best SaaS companies rather than to normalising-growth software; and competitive consolidation in which the SASE/SSE market narrows to two or three surviving platforms, with Zscaler's cloud-native architecture securing first-mover entrenchment. In this scenario, fiscal 2027 revenue approaches $4 billion, FCF margins cross thirty percent, and the stock recovers to a 13–15x NTM multiple. The resulting enterprise value of $48–55 billion, net of debt and plus cash, supports a share price in the $265–310 range.

**Base case — EV/NTM Revenue 9–10x, implied equity ~$185–215 per share.** Growth continues at eighteen to twenty-two percent annually. Free cash flow margins drift from the current mid-twenties to the high-twenties by fiscal 2027. The multiple holds in the current range, reflecting steady profitable growth without a re-rating catalyst. In this scenario the stock generates market-rate returns — roughly in line with the S&P 500 tech sector — without delivering the multiple expansion that transforms a good company into a market-beating investment. Fiscal 2026 revenue of approximately ~~$3.1 billion~~ ==$3.31 billion==, at 9.5x EV/NTM, supports an enterprise value near ~~$29 billion~~ ==$31 billion== and equity near ~~$200~~ ==$210== per share.

**Bear case — EV/NTM Revenue 6–7x, implied equity ~$130–150 per share.** The bear argument is that Palo Alto Networks' platformisation strategy — bundling equivalent SSE and SASE capabilities into existing firewall relationships at deeply discounted prices — proves more effective than Zscaler's stand-alone pure-play pitch in a cost-rationalisation environment. Billings growth decelerates to low-teens, large-deal slippage persists, and the market re-rates the stock toward Fortinet-parity multiples. At 6.5x forward revenue on a ~~$3.1 billion~~ ==$3.31 billion== fiscal 2026 estimate, enterprise value falls to approximately ~~$20 billion~~ ==$21.5 billion==, implying equity in the $135–150 range.

## Consensus versus the Dossier's Read

The Street consensus as of the frozen window was anchored in the base-to-mild-bull range, with most estimates clustering around $215–240 on a twelve-month basis — implying modest multiple recovery alongside continued revenue growth. The dossier's read is marginally more cautious on near-term re-rating, for a specific reason: the billings-to-revenue conversion cycle remains the central unresolved tension in the investment thesis. Revenue has been reliable; billings have been the source of repeated disappointment. Until Zscaler demonstrates two or three consecutive quarters of billings growth that comfortably exceeds revenue growth — the sign that the sales pipeline is building rather than drawing down — the market is unlikely to re-award the premium multiple that the platform's long-term competitive position might otherwise justify. The intrinsic value is not in dispute. The timing of the market's recognition of it is.

chapters.title: Multi-year trajectory through platform expansion and AI security pivot
chapters.body:
Between fiscal 2022 and fiscal 2025, Zscaler traced one of enterprise software's more instructive arcs: from hyper-growth security niche player to a $2.67 billion revenue business anchored by a platform that Jay Chaudhry was deliberately stretching far beyond its original perimeter. Revenue grew roughly fourfold across those four years, annual recurring revenue crossed $3 billion, and non-GAAP net income reached $534.8 million in fiscal 2025 — figures that, taken together, validated the proposition Chaudhry had pressed since the 2007 founding: that security belonged in the cloud, not bolted to the edge of a network.

The four-year trajectory ran through a distinct sequence of inflection points — a billion-dollar revenue crossing, an ARR doubling within two years, a measured deceleration in growth rates as the law of large numbers reasserted itself, a brief go-to-market reckoning, and ultimately a strategic reorientation toward artificial intelligence that repositioned the company not merely as a defender of enterprise infrastructure but as an operator of what Chaudhry called an AI-driven security operations platform.

## The $1 Billion Crossing: FY2022 and the Hyper-Growth Phase

Fiscal 2022, which ended 31 July 2022, established the commercial footing on which every subsequent milestone rested. Revenue reached $1.091 billion, a 62 percent increase on the prior year, crossing the symbolic billion-dollar threshold that separates growth-phase SaaS businesses from enterprise-scale platforms. The fourth quarter alone produced $318.1 million in revenue, with calculated billings of $520.4 million rising 57 percent year-over-year, and deferred revenue crossing $1 billion for the first time.

The operational discipline accompanying that growth attracted particular attention. The company achieved what Chaudhry described as the "Rule of 80" — the sum of revenue growth rate and operating margin reaching or exceeding eighty — for both the fourth quarter and the full fiscal year, a threshold that signalled the business had found leverage in its cost structure even as it added headcount and data-centre capacity at pace.

> "We delivered outstanding results for the fourth quarter with 61% revenue growth and 57% billings growth year over year, while driving operational efficiency across the company and delivering on Rule of 80 for the quarter and for the full year."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2022 earnings release, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2022](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368322000073/zs-07312022_991.htm)

The macro environment in calendar 2022 — rising interest rates, a sharp repricing of growth equities — did little to dent customer demand. Zero trust had passed from buzzword to budget-line item following a sequence of high-profile breaches, and Zscaler Internet Access and Zscaler Private Access, the ZIA and ZPA core modules, were increasingly the default architecture recommendation of enterprise security consultants.

## The ARR Doubling: FY2023's Record Performance

Fiscal 2023 produced what Chaudhry characterised as the fastest ARR doubling in the company's history. Revenue grew to $1.617 billion, a 48 percent increase, and the Q4 result — $455.0 million, up 43 percent — pushed ARR past the $2 billion mark. Billings in the fourth quarter reached $719.3 million, a 38 percent year-over-year advance, while deferred revenue grew 41 percent to $1.44 billion, suggesting the subscription base was being locked in at an accelerating rate.

Non-GAAP profitability improved materially, with non-GAAP net income of $100.9 million in Q4 FY2023 compared with $36.4 million in the equivalent quarter a year earlier.

> "We concluded our fiscal year with strong top line growth and record operating profits. In less than two years, we doubled our annual recurring revenue, surpassing the $2 billion milestone."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2023 earnings release, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2023](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368323000099/zs-07312023_991.htm)

Chaudhry pointed to the enterprise modernisation cycle as the durable demand driver. IT decision-makers were retiring hardware-based security stacks — firewalls, VPN concentrators, on-premises proxies — and replacing them with cloud-native equivalents. Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange, the cloud switchboard through which customer traffic was routed and inspected, was positioned as the architectural successor to that hardware estate.

> "With cyber security as a high priority, IT executives are modernizing their legacy network security with our zero-trust architecture. Our customers are realizing tremendous value from the new services and advanced capabilities delivered on our Zero Trust Exchange™ platform."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2023, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2023](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368323000099/zs-07312023_991.htm)

## The Platform Investment Cycle: FY2024

Fiscal 2024 brought a deliberate deceleration in reported growth rates as Zscaler absorbed the consequences of its own scale, while simultaneously making the acquisitions and executive appointments that would define the next strategic phase. Revenue rose 34 percent to $2.167 billion. The fourth quarter produced $592.9 million in revenue — 30 percent growth — with billings of $910.8 million and ARR crossing $2.5 billion. The customer base exceeded 8,650, including roughly 35 percent of the Forbes Global 2000, and the dollar-based net retention rate held at 115 percent, indicating that existing customers continued to expand their Zscaler footprints. Cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments stood at $2.41 billion as of 31 July 2024, [per the FY2024 10-K filed with the SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368324000109/zs-20240731.htm).

The most strategically significant transaction of the year was the March 2024 acquisition of Avalor Technologies, a security data management business whose Data Fabric for Security product ingested, normalised and unified data across enterprise security and business systems through more than 150 pre-built integrations. Chaudhry's rationale connected the acquisition directly to the AI capability arms race that was reshaping vendor positioning across the enterprise software industry.

> "AI is only as good as the underlying data, and many solutions lack the additional context and knowledge from data sources across the enterprise to truly leverage security specific AI models. Zscaler operates the world's largest security cloud with the most relevant data to train security specific large language models and with the Avalor acquisition, we can more effectively identify vulnerabilities, while predicting and preventing breaches."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Avalor acquisition announcement, [March 14 2024](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/future-security-risk-management-and-operations-data-and-ai)

By the close of fiscal 2024, the platform was processing more than half a trillion transactions daily — a data scale that Chaudhry argued was intrinsically valuable for training security-specific AI models. Closing the year, he signalled a shift in organisational emphasis from pure growth to go-to-market precision:

> "We ended a successful Fiscal 2024 with Q4 results exceeding the high end of our guidance across all metrics. I'm excited about the year ahead, as we enter Fiscal 2025 with a strong go-to-market machine and a high pace of innovation."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2024 earnings release, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368324000097/zs-07312024_991.htm)

## The AI Security Pivot: FY2025 and the $3 Billion Threshold

| Metric | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue ($B) | 1.091 | 1.617 | 2.167 | 2.673 |
| YoY Revenue Growth | +62% | +48% | +34% | +23% |
| ARR at year-end | — | $2.0B+ | $2.5B+ | $3.015B |
| Non-GAAP Net Income | $36.4M (Q4) | $100.9M (Q4) | $414.6M (FY) | $534.8M (FY) |
| GAAP Net Loss (FY) | — | — | ($57.7M) | ($41.5M) |

*Sources: [SEC 8-K filings, FY2022–FY2025](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001713683&type=8-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40)*

Fiscal 2025 opened with a sequential improvement in go-to-market execution that Chaudhry acknowledged directly. First-quarter revenue of $628.0 million grew 26 percent, with Chaudhry noting that "growing customer engagements and strong sales execution drove a solid Q1 with all metrics exceeding our guidance." The second quarter — $648 million in revenue, 23 percent growth, ARR of $2.7 billion — carried additional signal: the cohort of customers spending more than $1 million in annual recurring revenue reached 620, up 25 percent year-over-year, a metric that indicated the platform's expansion modules were gaining traction at the large-enterprise tier.

Data protection was one of the clearest upsell vectors: net new annual contract value in that category grew more than 40 percent year-over-year, and 85 percent of customers in the $1 million ARR cohort had adopted two or more data protection modules; 65 percent had adopted three or more. Zscaler Digital Experience, the performance-monitoring pillar of the platform, produced ZDX Copilot bookings of approximately $50 million in Q2 FY2025, up 45 percent. Chaudhry framed the breadth of the platform as a structural competitive differentiator, taking aim at the Secure Access Service Edge category that several rivals had staked out:

> "We have gone far beyond SASE by pioneering our zero trust exchange. Simply put, we offer better security at lower cost."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q2 FY2025 earnings call, [March 5 2025](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2025/03/05/zscaler-zs-q2-2025-earnings-call-transcript/)

## The $5 Billion Mandate and the Platform's Third Act

The ambition behind the platform expansion was formalised in September 2024 when Zscaler appointed Adam Geller, a security product veteran, as Chief Product Officer, in a hire explicitly positioned around scaling the business to $5 billion in ARR and beyond. Chaudhry framed Geller's task as building an AI-driven security operations platform — a second architectural layer atop the Zero Trust Exchange. In the same period, the company appointed Phil Tee, a co-founder of enterprise AI monitoring businesses, as Executive Vice President of AI Innovations, and acquired SPLX, a prompt-injection and AI security technology business, to seed the AI Guard product line.

By the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, the shape of that third act was visible in operating metrics. Revenue grew 21 percent to $719.2 million, ARR crossed $3.015 billion — up 22 percent — and the company posted its highest quarterly operating margin on record, exceeding 22 percent. Chaudhry's characterisation of the demand environment reflected the degree to which AI exposure had become the defining customer anxiety:

> "Zscaler's Zero Trust and AI security solutions are imperative in today's world and are driving robust demand. We recently delivered AI Guardrails for Public and Private apps, and we are rapidly expanding our AI security portfolio to address the emerging risks of AI models and applications."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2025 earnings release, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368325000138/zs-07312025_991.htm)

Across four fiscal years, Zscaler had scaled from a cloud-native proxy business chiefly selling ZIA and ZPA to an integrated platform whose emerging product lines — AI security, data protection, digital experience monitoring — were by management's account growing at twice the rate of the core. Full-year non-GAAP net income reached $534.8 million against a GAAP net loss that had narrowed to $41.5 million, suggesting the operating leverage inherent in a subscription SaaS model was finally expressing itself at scale. The transition from growth-at-all-costs to growth-with-demonstrated-economics, which Chaudhry had begun signalling with the Rule of 80 commitment in fiscal 2022, had completed its first cycle — and a second, AI-inflected cycle was already underway.

---

chapters.title: Jay Chaudhry, CFO, executive team, and the board
chapters.body:
## The Founder: From Himachal Pradesh to Silicon Valley

Jay Chaudhry's biography reads, in his own telling, as a parable about the inadequacy of perimeter security long before he coined the phrase. He was born on 26 August 1958 in Panoh, a village of roughly eight hundred people in what is now Himachal Pradesh. Electricity and running water did not reach Panoh until he was a teenager; he walked nearly four kilometres each morning to attend school in the neighbouring village. From that starting point, he earned a Bachelor of Technology in Electronics Engineering from IIT BHU Varanasi, then immigrated to the United States at age twenty-two, completing master's degrees in industrial engineering, computer engineering, and marketing at the University of Cincinnati before later attending Harvard Business School's executive management programme. The arc — from a village without a grid to the boardrooms of IBM, Unisys, and NCR, and then to founding five security companies — gives Chaudhry a biographical claim that few enterprise-software CEOs can match: a visceral understanding of what it means to operate without infrastructure that others take for granted. At sixty-seven, he remained Zscaler's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer as of the frozen snapshot date, having held both titles without interruption since the company's founding in 2007.

## Serial Founder: Four Exits Before Zscaler

The four companies Chaudhry built and sold before Zscaler form a coherent curriculum in the threat landscape that would eventually motivate zero trust. In 1996 he and his wife Jyoti founded **SecureIT**, described by Chaudhry as "the first pure-play Internet security service"; VeriSign acquired it in 1998. Two years later he launched **CipherTrust**, which developed what Zscaler describes as the industry's first email security gateway — a business eventually acquired by Secure Computing Corporation in 2006 for $274 million. In parallel he founded **CoreHarbor**, a managed e-commerce platform that AT&T subsidiary USi acquired. In 2002 he added **AirDefense**, a wireless-intrusion-detection pioneer; Motorola absorbed it in 2008. The pattern across all four was the same: identify an emerging threat vector — internet traffic, email, wireless — build a product that addressed it, and sell to a larger incumbent whose distribution could scale the technology. What that pattern never produced, in Chaudhry's view, was security designed for the cloud from the outset. The legacy platforms that acquired his companies bolted internet-security features onto architectures built around physical network perimeters. Zscaler was conceived to make that architecture obsolete.

## The 2007 Founding Thesis and the 2018 IPO

Chaudhry founded Zscaler in San Jose in 2007 with the explicit goal of building what he described as a security platform whose architecture mirrored how cloud services were delivered — not appliances sitting at a network edge, but a global network of enforcement nodes that traffic passes through regardless of where users or applications reside. The Zero Trust Exchange, as the platform came to be called, would eliminate the concept of an implicit trusted network entirely. Zscaler filed its S-1 with the SEC in February 2018 and began trading on NASDAQ under the ticker ZS on 16 March 2018, pricing at $16 per share — a valuation that was, at the time, considered rich for a company generating $190.7 million in revenue in the fiscal year ended 31 July 2018. The IPO validated the architecture thesis at a moment when enterprise migration to cloud services was accelerating and VPN-dependent remote-access architectures were showing their age. By fiscal year 2025, the same company reported full-year revenue of ~~$2.17 billion~~ ==$2.673 billion== with an ARR milestone that Chaudhry cited personally in the Q4 FY2025 earnings release:

> "We had an outstanding Q4, in which we achieved a new milestone of more than $3 billion of Annual Recurring Revenue while achieving our highest ever operating margin for a quarter. We believe Zscaler's Zero Trust and AI security solutions are imperative in today's world and are driving robust demand."

## The CFO Transition: Canessa to Rubin

For much of Zscaler's public life, Remo Canessa served as Chief Financial Officer, steering the company through the IPO and the hypergrowth years of fiscal 2019–2023. In 2024 Canessa announced his intention to retire; he remained with Zscaler in an advisory capacity through the end of fiscal year 2025 (31 July 2025) to support the handover. His successor, **Kevin Rubin**, joined Zscaler as CFO on 26 May 2025. Rubin, then fifty-one, brought a specific profile: more than two decades at high-growth public and private technology companies, including eight years as CFO of Alteryx (April 2016–March 2024), during which he also served as interim CEO from January to March 2024, and a subsequent year as CFO of BetterUp. His compensation on appointment was set at a $470,000 annual base salary and a $470,000 target annual bonus under the Employee Incentive Plan, with additional equity grants approved by the Compensation Committee. The hire landed at a pivotal moment — Zscaler was in the first full year of its transition from pure billings-growth narrative to a combined revenue-growth-plus-margin story, and Rubin's public-company operating experience at Alteryx, itself a business that navigated a significant go-to-market reconfiguration, was directly relevant.

## Operating Leadership

Below the CEO and CFO, the operating layer that executed the platform strategy as of the frozen date comprised:

| Executive | Title | Notable Prior Context |
|---|---|---|
| Kevin Rubin | Chief Financial Officer | CFO Alteryx 2016–2024; CFO BetterUp 2024–2025 |
| Adam Geller | Chief Product Officer | Internal Zscaler product leader, age 49 |
| Mike Rich | Chief Revenue Officer & President, Global Sales | Age 58; global enterprise sales leadership |
| ~~Raj Judge~~ | ~~EVP, Corporate Strategy & Ventures~~ | ~~Former Wilson Sonsini Senior Partner; joined May 2025~~ |
| Robert Schlossman | Chief Legal Officer & Secretary | Age 57; Zscaler general counsel |

Raj Judge's appointment in May 2025 was notable in that Zscaler structured his role explicitly to lead growth strategy, business development, and venture investment initiatives — and simultaneously added him to the board as a Class III director. ~~The dual executive-director status made Judge one of two non-independent directors alongside Chaudhry himself.~~ ==Judge resigned as officer and director effective April 15, 2026, leaving Chaudhry as the sole non-independent director on the board at the snapshot date.==

## The Board

The board that oversaw Zscaler as of the frozen date comprised ~~nine~~ ==eight== members, seven of them independent under Nasdaq standards. Three classes of directors serve staggered three-year terms, with the January 2026 annual meeting electing Class II directors Andrew Brown, Scott Darling, and David Schneider for terms running to the company's fiscal 2028 annual meeting.

| Director | Independence | Tenure on Board | Principal Credential |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jay Chaudhry | Non-independent | Since founding (2007) | Chairman, CEO, Founder |
| ~~Raj Judge~~ | ~~Non-independent~~ | ~~May 2025~~ | ~~EVP Corporate Strategy; former Wilson Sonsini~~ |
| Karen Blasing | Independent | January 2017 | Four-time CFO (Guidewire, Nuance, Force10, Salesforce SVP Finance); Audit Committee Chair |
| Charles Giancarlo | Independent | November 2016 | CEO, Pure Storage; former Cisco EVP; former Silver Lake MD |
| Scott Darling | Independent | November 2016 | President, Dell Technologies Capital; former Intel Capital VP/MD |
| Andrew Brown | Independent | 2015 | Longest-tenured independent director |
| David Schneider | Independent | — | President, Global Customer Operations, ServiceNow; former CRO, ServiceNow |
| Eileen Naughton | Independent | September 2021 | Former Chief People Officer, Google; board member, Ares Management |
| James Beer | Independent | May 2024 | Former CFO, Atlassian; board member, Alaska Air Group, DocuSign |

**Karen Blasing** chairs the Audit Committee and brings the deepest financial governance credentials on the board — four CFO tenures including Guidewire Software, where she led the company's January 2012 IPO and two follow-on offerings. Her presence since January 2017 means she has overseen the Zscaler IPO process alongside Canessa from the governance side. **Charles Giancarlo**, the longest-serving independent director, joined in November 2016, just over a year before the S-1 was filed; his background running the product lines that generated roughly 80 percent of Cisco's revenues in the mid-2000s, and his subsequent CEO role at Pure Storage, gave the board direct hyperscaler-era operating experience. **James Beer**, added in May 2024, deepened the bench of financial expertise at a moment when Zscaler's investors were increasingly focused on margin progression and free-cash-flow generation — his Atlassian CFO tenure coincided with that company's own transition from hypergrowth to scaled-profitability narrative. **Eileen Naughton**'s background as Google's Chief People Officer addresses the talent-governance dimension as Zscaler expanded headcount aggressively through its platform-broadening phase.

## Ownership and Control

The 2025 proxy statement filed in November 2025 disclosed that Chaudhry beneficially owned 26,857,608 shares directly, representing approximately 16.8 percent of shares outstanding as of 1 November 2025. ~~Including indirect holdings through family trusts and affiliated entities, his total beneficial ownership has been estimated at approximately 38 percent of the outstanding stock — a concentration that gives the founder substantial practical influence over matters put to a shareholder vote, even absent a formal dual-class share structure.~~ ==This 16.8 percent stake, held by a founder who is also full-time CEO and chairman, gives Chaudhry substantial practical influence over matters put to a shareholder vote, even absent a formal dual-class share structure.== Zscaler's capital structure is single-class common stock, which means Chaudhry's voting power derives from raw economic ownership rather than super-voting shares; nonetheless, at ~~roughly 38 percent~~ ==approximately 16.8 percent== held by a founder who is also full-time CEO and chairman, the governance dynamic at Zscaler ~~more closely resembles a founder-controlled company than a widely dispersed institutional-ownership base~~ ==retains a meaningful founder-influence character relative to a widely dispersed institutional-ownership base==, even at a $20-billion-plus market capitalisation. The 2025 proxy noted the board's awareness of the concentration and the Compensation Committee's effort to align long-term equity vesting schedules across the executive team with multi-year performance objectives rather than pure time-based vesting — a structural acknowledgement that succession and ownership-dilution management are active governance questions as the platform matures.

---

*Sources: [Zscaler DEF 14A FY2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368325000198/zs-20251121.htm) · [Zscaler 8-K Q4 FY2025 earnings](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368325000138/zs-07312025_991.htm) · [Zscaler 8-K CFO appointment (Kevin Rubin)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368325000078/zs-04302025_992.htm) · [Zscaler Jay Chaudhry biography](https://www.zscaler.com/company/leadership/jay-chaudhry) · [GlobeNewswire — James Beer appointment](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2024/05/28/2889447/0/en/Zscaler-Appoints-Veteran-Finance-Executive-James-Beer-to-its-Board-of-Directors.html) · [Zscaler — Eileen Naughton appointment](https://www.zscaler.com/press/zscaler-appoints-industry-veteran-eileen-naughton-its-board-directors) · [Zscaler — Raj Judge appointment](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/raj-judge-joins-zscalers-board-directors-and-evp-corporate)*

chapters.title: Enterprise, federal, partner channel, go-to-market motion
chapters.body:
## Enterprise Customer Architecture

Zscaler built its commercial engine around a deliberately concentrated targeting strategy: sell the Global 2000 — the world's two thousand largest corporations by revenue — on replacing their network-security perimeter not with better hardware, but with none at all. By the time the company reported fiscal 2024 results in September 2024, that proposition had translated into roughly 8,700 customers and annual revenue of ~~$2.167 billion~~ ==$2.168 billion==, a customer base whose composition, increasingly skewed toward multimillion-dollar relationships and US federal agencies, reflected a platform that had escaped commodity positioning and lodged itself in enterprise procurement as a strategic asset.

The consequences of Global 2000 targeting are most legible in the large-customer cohort disclosures Zscaler included in its SEC filings. In fiscal 2022, approximately 340 customers generated more than $1 million in annual recurring revenue, against a total base of roughly 6,700. By fiscal 2024, those figures had grown to approximately 560 customers above the $1 million threshold and more than 34 customers above $5 million, while the total customer count reached approximately 8,700. The widening gap — total customers growing roughly 15% annually while million-dollar customers expanded faster — reflected both the platform's success in winning larger initial deployments and the land-and-expand dynamic as customers layered data-protection and AI-security modules atop the ZIA and ZPA core.

[Zscaler 10-K, fiscal year ended July 31 2024, filed September 2024 via SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=ZS&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=10)

The named-account model that underpinned this concentrated customer base required a corresponding sales architecture. Enterprise account executives were assigned defined Global 2000 territories and paired with solution architects; a post-sale customer-success function tracked workload deployment depth and module adoption. New logo acquisition was prized, but the subscription economics meant that expansion within the installed base was the dominant revenue-growth lever in any given quarter.

## The Federal Beachhead

No segment illustrated Zscaler's concentrated-customer thesis more sharply than the US federal government, where a single executive order and one procurement tier reshaped the company's pipeline in the early 2020s.

President Biden's May 2021 cybersecurity executive order mandated that federal agencies migrate toward zero-trust architectures within defined timescales.
