Zscaler had by that point obtained FedRAMP High authorization — the most demanding compliance tier for cloud vendors supplying sensitive federal workloads — positioning it ahead of competitors whose federal authorizations remained at the more common FedRAMP Moderate level. FedRAMP High certification, which covers systems handling data classified as high-impact under federal risk-management standards, was a prerequisite for many agency engagements and a material barrier against rivals seeking to enter the federal zero-trust market.

The Defense Information Systems Agency, which manages network-security infrastructure for the Department of Defense, became one of Zscaler's most visible federal reference customers. Multiple civilian agencies followed under the post-executive-order zero-trust migration mandate, and by fiscal 2024 the federal segment was disclosed as a meaningful and growing contributor to total ARR, though Zscaler did not break out a standalone federal revenue figure in its 10-K filings. The company's FedRAMP High authorization also served a secondary commercial function: demonstrating to regulated commercial enterprises — banks, healthcare systems, critical-infrastructure operators — that the Zero Trust Exchange met the most stringent data-handling requirements available under US federal standards.

The FY2025 period introduced new variables. The second Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency initiative, announced in early 2025, created uncertainty over discretionary federal IT spending, and agency workforce reductions compressed procurement timelines at several departments. Zscaler's management acknowledged the federal demand environment had become less predictable but argued that agency zero-trust mandates remained embedded in departmental IT roadmaps as structural compliance obligations rather than optional spending — a contention supported by the DoD's own published zero-trust framework, which named cloud-delivered security-as-a-service as an architectural pillar.

## Partner Channel Architecture

Zscaler's relationship with the global systems-integrator community evolved from limited early engagement into a structured co-selling and co-delivery apparatus. By fiscal 2023 and 2024, the most significant SI relationships — Accenture, Deloitte, IBM, Wipro, Infosys, Capgemini, and Tata Consultancy Services among them — were generating partner-influenced pipeline across both new-logo and expansion transactions. These firms trained dedicated Zscaler practices, embedded certified Zero Trust Exchange architects within client engagement teams, and increasingly positioned Zscaler deployments as the security layer inside broader cloud-migration and digital-transformation mandates.

The strategic significance of SI influence was structural. A Global 2000 corporation launching a multi-year cloud infrastructure transformation typically selected a primary systems integrator before selecting individual security vendors; the SI's architectural recommendation could pre-qualify Zscaler or, conversely, entrench a competitor. Zscaler's investment in the partner ecosystem — certification programs, co-marketing funding, joint go-to-market commitments, and dedicated partner-success managers — was as much defensive as it was a new-logo acquisition play.

Managed security service providers formed a distinct channel layer. MSSPs resold and operated the Zero Trust Exchange on behalf of mid-market and enterprise customers lacking internal security-operations resources, extending Zscaler's commercial reach below its direct enterprise sales ceiling. Technology alliances deepened the platform's competitive moat: a joint Zscaler–CrowdStrike deployment correlated zero-trust network telemetry with endpoint-detection data, while integrations with Okta anchored identity-aware access policies to the Zero Trust Exchange enforcement layer. ServiceNow integrations connected Zscaler's risk signals to enterprise IT service-management workflows, making the platform stickier inside large accounts where ServiceNow was already embedded.

Value-added resellers — CDW, Presidio, Insight, and similar North American distributors — handled transactional volume and mid-market coverage, freeing the direct enterprise team to focus on named Global 2000 accounts and large-deal origination.

## Net Retention and the Land-and-Expand Engine

Zscaler's subscription model concentrated financial-performance risk in a single underlying metric: net revenue retention — the proportion of prior-year ARR that renewed and expanded in the current period. The company had historically reported NRR in excess of 120%, indicating that expansions and upsells materially outweighed churn. In later fiscal periods Zscaler shifted public disclosure toward cohort-based large-customer metrics rather than a single consolidated NRR figure, but the operative dynamic remained unchanged: customers initiated deployment with ZIA or ZPA, proved out the architecture in a defined pilot population, and then progressively expanded to ZDX performance monitoring, data-loss prevention, cloud-access security broker functionality, and emerging AI-security and IoT/OT modules.

The pillar-expansion model was integral to the financial pitch to CFOs. An enterprise that had already amortized Zscaler's client-connector deployment and invested in policy migration could add a data-protection pillar at incremental cost and disruption; the marginal economics of adding a SaaS module onto existing infrastructure justified Zscaler's premium relative to point-solution competitors. By fiscal 2024, Zscaler disclosed that a growing share of its customer base consumed three or more product pillars — a metric management cited as evidence of platform stickiness over and above basic renewal rates.

| Customer Cohort Metric | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total customers | ~6,700 | ~7,700 | ~8,700 |
| Customers >$1M ARR | ~340 | ~430 | ~560 |
| Customers >$5M ARR | — | — | >34 |
| Revenue (USD) | $1.091B | $1.617B | ~~$2.167B~~ ==$2.168B== |

*Source: Zscaler 10-K filings, SEC EDGAR*

## Go-to-Market Evolution Into the AI Era

As the fiscal 2025 period opened, Zscaler's go-to-market motion began adapting to a selling environment reshaped by enterprise AI adoption. The proliferation of large-language-model workloads within Global 2000 accounts created demand for security controls specific to AI: protection against data leakage through SaaS-based AI applications, governance over which third-party AI services employees could access, and inspection of API traffic flowing between internal systems and external model endpoints. Zscaler's AI security suite — positioned atop the existing Zero Trust Exchange inline-inspection infrastructure — was marketed as the natural extension of an already-deployed platform, a framing designed to convert the installed base rather than open new competitive evaluations from scratch.

Jay Chaudhry framed the AI moment as a demand accelerant on fiscal 2025 earnings calls, arguing that enterprise AI adoption created fresh urgency around inline traffic inspection and data governance — precisely the capabilities the Zero Trust Exchange had been built to deliver at scale.

The go-to-market motion that had carried Zscaler from founding to $2 billion in revenue — direct enterprise selling into the Global 2000, backed by SI partnerships and an expanding land-and-expand installed base — entered the AI era carrying the structural advantages of incumbency: enforcement infrastructure already deployed across customer networks, trust relationships established through years of subscription renewals, and a cloud-native inline architecture uniquely positioned to inspect the AI-era traffic patterns its enterprise customers were only beginning to generate at volume.

chapters.title: Where Zscaler sits against Palo Alto Prisma, Netskope, Cisco, Cloudflare
chapters.body:
By the time Zscaler's annual recurring revenue crossed $3 billion in mid-fiscal 2025, the company had spent nearly two decades arguing a single architectural proposition: that security should live in the cloud, inline between users and applications, rather than in hardware stacked in corporate data centres. That proposition was, by the spring of 2026, no longer controversial. It had become the organising thesis of the entire enterprise security market — which meant every major vendor in that market was now competing directly with Zscaler.

The competitive field that formed around Zscaler was varied in origin but convergent in ambition. Palo Alto Networks attacked from the established security incumbency, leveraging its dominant firewall franchise and a $6.33 billion Next-Generation Security ARR base to assemble a rival SASE platform. Netskope, a cloud-native proxy pure-play that finally reached public markets in September 2025, contested the same blue-chip enterprise logos with differentiated data-loss prevention. Cisco brought its vast installed networking base and bundling leverage — and the sales reach of 60,000-plus enterprise relationships. Cloudflare arrived from a different direction entirely, building zero-trust access on top of a global content-delivery network that already touched the internet at scale. And behind those four principals, a longer tail of vendors — Forcepoint, Skyhigh Security, Check Point Harmony SASE, Lookout — competed for mid-market share and specialised verticals.

## The Principal Rival: Palo Alto Networks Prisma

No competitive pairing drew more analyst attention through 2025 and into 2026 than Zscaler versus Palo Alto Networks. The two companies had roughly comparable revenues — Zscaler reported $2.673 billion for fiscal year 2025 against Palo Alto's full-year guidance of $11.3 billion, though Palo Alto's total included network security, cloud security, and a large on-premises installed base — but in the specific SASE/SSE contest, the numbers converged more closely. Palo Alto's SASE ARR reached $1.5 billion in the fiscal second quarter of 2026, growing approximately 40 per cent year-on-year, against Zscaler's total company ARR of $3.4 billion growing 25 per cent. The two vendors were, in market-analyst parlance, trading at different multiples on different base sizes, but both were compounding faster than the broader security market.

| Vendor | ARR / NGS ARR (most recent Q) | YoY Growth | Gartner MQ Position |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zscaler | $3.4B (Q2 FY2026, Jan 2026) | +25% | SSE Leader (1st) |
| Palo Alto SASE only | $1.5B (Q2 FY2026, Jan 2026) | ~+40% | SASE / SSE / SD-WAN Leader |
| Netskope | $754M ARR (Q3 FY2026, Oct 2025) | +34% | SSE Leader / Forrester highest |
| Cloudflare | ~$2.4B total rev. run-rate | +31–34% | SASE Visionary |

Palo Alto's competitive pitch rested on two pillars: breadth and depth. Its Prisma Access platform carried the full Layer 7 inspection capability of a next-generation firewall into the cloud, offering packet-level visibility that Palo Alto's marketing teams positioned as superior to what they called Zscaler's "proxy-overlay" approach. Prisma Browser added a natively integrated enterprise browser — serving more than 1,500 enterprise customers with over nine million licences by early 2026 — a capability Zscaler did not match organically, though the company moved to address the gap through its acquisition of browser-security startup SquareX. Palo Alto was, critically, the only vendor recognised as a Gartner Magic Quadrant leader in all three adjacent categories simultaneously: SASE, SSE, and SD-WAN, a distinction its sales teams weaponised in competitive evaluations. The company's [second-quarter FY2026 investor materials](https://www.investing.com/news/company-news/palo-alto-networks-q2-2026-slides-ngs-arr-jumps-33-stock-falls-5-93CH-4511827) showed 1,100-plus "platformized" customers — accounts that had consolidated four or more Palo Alto product families — as evidence that the consolidation trade was going its way.

## Architecture as the Core Argument

Against Palo Alto's firepower, Zscaler returned again and again to architecture. The company's Zero Trust Exchange, built cloud-natively from its 2007 founding rather than cloudified from hardware, operated across more than 150 points of presence and 160 data centres globally by 2025, processing hundreds of billions of transactions per day in-line between users and destinations. The distinction mattered technically: a proxy-based inline model meant Zscaler could inspect, modify, and enforce policy on every byte of traffic traversing its platform, creating a telemetry reservoir that improved machine-learning models in a self-reinforcing loop. The scale of that reservoir — accumulated over eighteen years of cloud-only operation — was not easily replicated.

Jay Chaudhry framed the architectural bet in terms of the AI transition on Zscaler's first-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings call:

> "The best AI security is built on the foundation of Zero Trust."

And on the company's second-quarter call, as the proliferation of AI agents became the dominant enterprise-security narrative:

> "Enterprises will need 'inline policy enforcement at massive scale' as AI agents proliferate."

Zscaler's position was that Palo Alto's NGFW-in-the-cloud approach, however capable, was a different animal — a security inspection appliance delivered as a service rather than a purpose-built cloud fabric. Customers running Prisma Access still typically paired it with a third-party SD-WAN vendor, or with Palo Alto's own Prisma SD-WAN, adding integration complexity. Zscaler, by contrast, had always required no WAN hardware at the edge, and its [Zero Trust Branch](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-first-quarter-fiscal-2026-financial-results) segmentation product — introduced to isolate branch networks without traditional firewalls — extended that no-hardware premise further into campus and industrial environments.

## Netskope: The Pure-Play Challenger

Netskope occupied a narrower but genuine threat. The San Jose-based vendor filed for its initial public offering in August 2025, disclosing $707 million in ARR, growing 33 per cent year-on-year, and completed the offering in September at $19 per share, raising approximately $908 million. By the third fiscal quarter of 2026, ARR had reached $754 million, and the company reported a dollar-based net retention rate of 118 per cent against a base of roughly 4,300 customers, more than 100 of whom paid in excess of $1 million annually.

Netskope's differentiation centred on data security. Its inline Data Loss Prevention and Cloud Access Security Broker capabilities were consistently rated superior to Zscaler's by enterprise security teams in proof-of-concept evaluations, particularly in regulated industries where granular data classification mattered. Forrester's 2025 SASE Wave awarded Netskope the highest composite score among all vendors, ahead of Palo Alto and Zscaler, a recognition that carried weight in accounts where DLP was the primary buying criterion. The company had not, however, resolved its profitability challenge: full-year net losses reached $354.5 million in fiscal 2025, up from $344.9 million the prior year, a trajectory that post-IPO public-market investors would scrutinise closely. Zscaler, by contrast, had been generating positive non-GAAP operating income since fiscal 2020.

## Cisco: The Incumbent Bundler

Cisco's competitive relevance rested less on architectural innovation than on distribution leverage. The company's Cisco+ Secure Connect Now combined Meraki SD-WAN with Umbrella's Secure Service Edge capabilities into a single-vendor SASE offer — directly targeting the large installed base of enterprises already running Meraki campus switches and Catalyst SD-WAN across their branch networks. With more than 60,000 enterprise relationships worldwide and a global sales organisation that dwarfed any pure-play security vendor's, Cisco could attach security subscriptions to hardware refresh cycles in ways Zscaler, Netskope, or Cloudflare could not.

The financial picture, however, was complicated. Cisco's security segment grew 59 per cent in fiscal 2025, a figure inflated by the March 2024 acquisition of Splunk; stripped of that contribution, the underlying security business faced more modest growth, and by Q1 fiscal 2026 the security segment had turned negative year-on-year, declining 2 per cent. Enterprise buyers increasingly distinguished between Cisco's networking-rooted security stack — perceived as stitched-together from Umbrella, Duo, and Meraki acquisitions — and the architecturally coherent platforms of Zscaler or even Palo Alto. [Dell'Oro Group research](https://www.channelfutures.com/sdn-sd-wan/zscaler-palo-alto-networks-cisco-sase-market) identified Palo Alto, Cisco, and Zscaler as the top three vendors in SASE by revenue, but the gap between Cisco's legacy revenue and its cloud-native SASE bookings reflected a transition that remained incomplete.

## Cloudflare and the Network-Centric Insurgents

Cloudflare represented a qualitatively different threat: a vendor approaching zero-trust from the network infrastructure layer rather than from security inspection. Its Cloudflare One platform — combining ZTNA, SWG, CASB, and remote browser isolation — ran on the same global network that already handled a meaningful fraction of the internet's DNS and CDN traffic, giving it inherent performance advantages in latency-sensitive geographies. The company [reported](https://www.investing.com/news/company-news/cloudflare-q1-2026-slides-34-revenue-growth-large-customer-base-surges-93CH-4671018) 34 per cent revenue growth in Q1 2026 and signed what management described as the company's longest SASE contract during the first quarter of 2025. Gartner's 2025 SASE Magic Quadrant classified Cloudflare as a Visionary rather than a Leader — reflecting a platform that was still maturing in enterprise DLP and advanced threat-prevention depth — but the trajectory was upward. BTIG's late-2025 decision to downgrade Zscaler to Neutral, citing "intensifying zero-trust competition," specifically named Cloudflare alongside Netskope as the sources of incremental competitive pressure in the small-to-mid enterprise segment.

## The Longer Tail

Beyond the four principals, a second tier of vendors competed for specific verticals and mid-market accounts. Check Point's Harmony SASE — rebranded and extended to include an enterprise browser in 2025 — earned a strong threat-prevention score in Miercom's 2025 benchmark and appealed to enterprises already standardised on Check Point's firewall estate. Forcepoint and Skyhigh Security (formerly McAfee Enterprise's cloud business, operating under Musarubra/Skyhigh's private-equity ownership) maintained loyal installed bases in data-centric verticals, particularly US federal government and financial services, where policy compliance requirements made their specialised DLP heritage compelling. Lookout served the mobile-centric SSE segment.

None of these vendors individually posed a systemic threat to Zscaler's enterprise motion, but collectively they ensured that competitive intensity across the full market remained high, compression on average selling prices remained a structural reality, and the number of evaluation criteria against which Zscaler had to defend continued to expand.

## The Structural Moat

Zscaler's most durable competitive asset was not any single product but the architecture itself — and the eighteen years of operational data that had accumulated inside it. Every transaction inspected, every policy enforced, every threat blocked added signal to the Zero Trust Exchange's machine-learning models. By early 2026 the company processed hundreds of billions of daily transactions across its global fabric; Chaudhry cited the company as well positioned to surpass $10 billion in ARR over the longer term, implying a belief that the Exchange's data-gravity advantage would compound faster than rivals could replicate it through platform assembly.

That thesis was coherent, though not without stress points. Palo Alto's NGS ARR trajectory — targeting $20 billion by 2030 on the back of its platformization strategy — and Netskope's DLP depth represented genuine architectural challenges to specific Zscaler customer segments. The market itself was growing fast enough — the SSE segment alone was projected by Grand View Research to expand at a 21.9 per cent compound annual rate from $6.26 billion in 2024 to $36.87 billion by 2033 — that multiple vendors could compound simultaneously without fighting purely zero-sum battles. But the platform consolidation pressure that had shrunk the long tail of point-product security vendors in the early 2020s was now pressing on the SASE layer itself. By May 2026, the question for Zscaler was not whether its architecture was sound, but whether it could expand broadly enough — into data security, AI operations, IoT segmentation, and managed detection — to remain the centre of gravity around which customers consolidated, rather than one pillar among many inside a larger Palo Alto or Cisco bundle.

---

chapters.title: Timeline from 2007 founding through 2018 IPO and platform expansion
chapters.body:
## A Serial Founder's Thesis, Crystallized

When Jay Chaudhry incorporated Zscaler in San Jose in 2007, he carried a thesis that the rest of the security industry had not yet accepted: the perimeter was already dead. Enterprises had begun migrating workloads to the internet and, soon, to cloud platforms; the corporate network as a defined boundary was becoming a fiction. Legacy firewall appliances and hardware proxies—products built to guard a physical perimeter—would prove inadequate in a world where users worked from anywhere and data lived everywhere.

The conviction was informed by hard-won entrepreneurial experience. Before Zscaler, Chaudhry had built and sold four security companies: SecureIT, acquired by VeriSign in 1998; CipherTrust, an email security firm sold to Tumbleweed Communications in 2006; AirDefense, a wireless security business later absorbed by Motorola Solutions; and CoreHarbor, a managed hosting provider. Each exit deepened his understanding of how enterprise security was being provisioned—and why point products delivered by appliance would lose the architectural battle to cloud-scale software.

The product architecture Chaudhry designed from the outset was deliberately different. Rather than intercepting traffic at a corporate network border, Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange would sit inline in the cloud, inspecting every packet traversing the internet from any device, anywhere. Users and applications would meet in Zscaler's cloud, never on a shared network segment. The security stack—proxy, firewall, sandboxing, data loss prevention—would be delivered as a service from globally distributed nodes, not from racks of hardware in a corporate data center.

## Building the Core Platform: ZIA and ZPA

The first commercially available product was Zscaler Internet Access, or ZIA, launched in the years following the founding. ZIA replaced enterprise web proxies and next-generation firewalls for internet-bound traffic, offering SSL inspection, URL filtering, and threat protection at cloud scale. The pitch to enterprise buyers was structural: ZIA cost less to operate than appliances, required no hardware refresh cycles, and scaled elastically as workforces grew or went remote.

The complementary product, Zscaler Private Access (ZPA), arrived in subsequent years and attacked a different appliance category: the virtual private network. Where VPNs granted authenticated users access to an entire network segment—creating lateral-movement risk for any attacker who obtained valid credentials—ZPA granted access only to specific named applications, with no network exposure. Users were connected to applications, not to networks.

Together, ZIA and ZPA constituted what Zscaler marketed as the foundational zero-trust architecture. The term "zero trust," popularized by Forrester Research analyst John Kindervag, aligned precisely with what Chaudhry had been building: no implicit trust, continuous verification, least-privilege access. Zscaler became the vendor most closely identified with zero-trust delivery at enterprise scale.

## The 2018 IPO: A Cloud Security Debut

On March 16, 2018, Zscaler listed on the NASDAQ under the ticker **ZS**, pricing its initial public offering at $16 per share and raising approximately $192 million in gross proceeds. The stock closed its first session near $33—a gain of roughly 106% on the IPO price—making it one of the strongest cybersecurity IPO debuts on record at that point, with a first-day market capitalization exceeding $4 billion.

The [S-1 filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001713683&type=S-1) ahead of the offering disclosed the then-current financial profile: subscription-only SaaS revenue, with billings as the primary growth indicator. At the time of listing, Zscaler was pre-GAAP-profitability but growing at rates that commanded premium valuation multiples. The company disclosed serving more than 2,800 customers worldwide and claimed inspection of more than 35 billion transactions per day—a figure that would multiply many times over in the years following the offering.

## Post-IPO Scaling and the COVID Inflection

The years between the 2018 IPO and fiscal 2021 produced strong but not yet transformative billings growth as Zscaler built out its enterprise go-to-market motion and expanded internationally. The secular thesis was being validated gradually—until March 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic forced hundreds of millions of corporate workers remote and overnight exposed the architectural deficiencies of VPN-centric and appliance-based security models.

Demand for ZPA accelerated sharply. Enterprise security teams that had evaluated but deferred zero-trust projects found themselves compelled to move. The pandemic-era pull-forward, combined with genuine platform adoption, pushed Zscaler's [fiscal 2021 revenue](https://ir.zscaler.com) to $673 million. By fiscal 2022, revenue crossed $1 billion for the first time at $1.091 billion—a threshold marking Zscaler's transition from growth-stage to scaled SaaS vendor.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD) | YoY Growth |
|---|---|---|
| FY2021 (ended July 2021) | $673M | ~56% |
| FY2022 (ended July 2022) | $1.091B | ~62% |
| FY2023 (ended July 2023) | $1.617B | ~48% |
| FY2024 (ended July 2024) | ~~$2.167B~~ ==$2.168B== | ~34% |

*Source: [Zscaler Investor Relations](https://ir.zscaler.com); [SEC EDGAR filings for ZS](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001713683&type=10-K)*

The deceleration in growth rate from FY2022 onward reflected both a larger revenue base and a normalization of pandemic-era demand—but the absolute trajectory remained compelling at this scale.

## Platform Expansion Beyond the Core Duopoly

By fiscal 2023 and 2024, the strategic narrative shifted from selling ZIA and ZPA as standalone products toward positioning the Zero Trust Exchange as a comprehensive platform. Zscaler Digital Experience (ZDX) addressed a specific enterprise pain point: visibility into application performance and end-user experience across cloud and hybrid environments. As ZIA and ZPA removed network-layer visibility tools that IT teams had relied upon, ZDX provided replacement telemetry—monitoring session quality, latency, and application health from the endpoint outward.

The data protection stack—incorporating cloud-native data loss prevention and cloud access security broker (CASB) capabilities—positioned Zscaler to capture budget previously allocated to point DLP and CASB vendors. Risk360, a unified risk management dashboard introduced in this period, offered board-level risk quantification alongside operational security telemetry, addressing governance and reporting needs that security leaders increasingly faced in a landscape of regulatory expansion and cyber insurance underwriting scrutiny.

## Federal Authorization and Channel Architecture

Zscaler's FedRAMP High authorization positioned the platform for U.S. federal government adoption at agencies with the most stringent compliance requirements. The federal market represented a differentiated opportunity: Office of Management and Budget directives mandated zero-trust architecture transitions across civilian agencies, creating a procurement cycle aligned precisely with Zscaler's architecture. Agencies required not merely zero-trust-adjacent products bolted onto legacy stacks, but a cloud-native architecture purpose-built for continuous verification—which was exactly what the Zero Trust Exchange delivered.

The partner channel—systems integrators, managed security service providers, and global consultancies—carried an increasing share of bookings as the platform matured. Channel-sourced deals often included implementation services delivered alongside the platform license, improving customer onboarding and retention economics.

## AI Security Operations: The 2024–2026 Catalyst

From fiscal 2024 forward, Chaudhry positioned AI as both a threat surface requiring control and an operational capability embedded in the platform. Generative AI adoption inside enterprises created a new category of data leakage risk—employees submitting proprietary information to large language model interfaces—and a new class of AI-assisted phishing and adversarial attack. Zscaler's inline inspection architecture, already sitting between users and the internet, was structurally positioned to inspect and govern AI application traffic without requiring additional deployment.

Simultaneously, AI and machine learning were embedded into platform operations: automated threat hunting, risk scoring, policy recommendation, and incident triage. IoT and operational technology (OT) security extended the zero-trust model to machine-to-machine traffic—factory floors, building automation, connected industrial systems—a segment that legacy network security tools handled poorly. Each expansion product enlarged the addressable contract value per existing customer, enabling net revenue retention above 100% and providing a platform-expansion flywheel alongside net new customer additions.

As of the fiscal 2024 close, with revenue at ~~$2.167 billion~~ ==$2.168 billion== and the platform expanding well beyond its ZIA/ZPA origins, Zscaler occupied a structural position as the cloud-native zero-trust pure-play at scale—a platform built on the proposition that in a world of distributed users, distributed applications, and distributed threats, the network perimeter had not merely weakened, but ceased to exist as a meaningful security construct.

chapters.title: Cloud-native architecture IP, zero-trust patents, R&D framework
chapters.body:
Jay Chaudhry's foundational decision in 2007 was architectural rather than commercial. While the established security industry was still debating cloud viability, Chaudhry designed Zscaler as a multi-tenant, cloud-native proxy — not a software layer draped over a physical appliance. That choice embedded durable intellectual property into the platform long before enterprise adoption caught up, and by the time rivals acknowledged the model's advantages, Zscaler had accumulated hundreds of issued patents, trade secrets, and operational infrastructure that proved resistant to compression into a catch-up development cycle.

## The Zero Trust Exchange as Engineering Infrastructure

The Zero Trust Exchange differed from legacy security architectures in one decisive respect: it processed traffic inline at the closest cloud point of presence rather than routing it to a central appliance or data centre perimeter. The platform's globally distributed network, spanning more than 150 data centres, simultaneously served as customer infrastructure, AI training corpus, and competitive barrier. By fiscal 2025, Zscaler reported processing more than half a trillion transactions daily — a data volume that compounded threat detection capabilities with each additional enterprise onboarded.

Zscaler Private Access relied on what the company described as an inside-out connectivity model: enterprise applications initiated outbound connections to the Zero Trust Exchange rather than exposing listening ports or IP addresses on the public internet. An authenticated attacker who compromised credentials still could not perform network reconnaissance — there was no perimeter address to scan. This design was sufficiently differentiated from VPN architectures that it anchored core patent claims filed during ZPA's development period.

## Patent Portfolio: Six Domains, Seventeen Years

As of the fiscal 2024 [Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368324000109/zs-20240731.htm) filed with the SEC in September 2024, Zscaler reported more than 580 issued patents and pending patent applications in the United States and internationally, including more than 260 issued patents. The portfolio's arc was visible in its numbering: patent 7,894,350, among the earliest on record, anchors the Cloud Protection category; the most recently numbered grants — 12,445,459 and 12,445,467 in the Security Operations and AI Security categories — reflect filings from the 2024–2025 period. Issued patents expire between 2028 and 2043.

The company's public patent registry at [zscaler.com/legal/patents](https://www.zscaler.com/legal/patents) organised the portfolio into six product-aligned domains:

| Patent Category | Associated Products | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud Protection | ZIA, Zero Trust Exchange, Posture Control, Workload Communications | 85+ patents |
| Zero Trust Networking | ZIA, ZPA, Zero Trust Branch, Zero Trust Browser | 60+ patents |
| Data Protection | Enterprise DLP, CASB, DSPM, Cloud Browser Isolation | 60+ patents |
| Cyber Threat Protection | ThreatLabz, ATP, Cloud Sandbox, Cloud Firewall, Cloud IPS | growing |
| Security Operations | Agentic SecOps, Deception, Unified Vulnerability Management | growing |
| Digital Experience & AI Security | ZDX, AI-Powered Segmentation, AI Red Teaming, AI Protect | growing |

Cloud Protection, at 85-plus patents, was the deepest tranche — reflecting the foundational nature of the inline proxy and multi-tenant cloud delivery design that underpinned the entire platform. Zscaler supplemented its patent position with copyright, trademark, and trade secret protections alongside contractual provisions in customer and employee agreements, per standard disclosures in successive 10-K filings.

## R&D Investment Trajectory

Zscaler sustained research and development spending well above the enterprise software industry median, treating the engineering cost base as a primary competitive investment. Per the [fiscal 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368324000109/zs-20240731.htm) and [fiscal 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm):

| Fiscal Year (ended July 31) | Revenue | R&D Expense | R&D % of Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | $1,091M | $289M | 26.5% |
| FY2023 | $1,617M | $350M | 21.6% |
| FY2024 | $2,168M | $500M | 23.1% |
| FY2025 | ~~$2,680M~~ ==$2,673M== | $673M | ~~25.1%~~ ==25.2%== |

The step-up from $500 million in fiscal 2024 to $673 million in fiscal 2025 — a 35 percent increase — reflected both organic headcount growth and the integration of engineering teams acquired through Avalor. The fiscal 2025 figure also included $4.8 million in restructuring charges related to employee severance within the R&D function.

The fiscal 2024 10-K identified principal engineering locations in San Jose (headquarters), India, Canada, Israel, and Spain — a footprint providing talent access across time zones and technical specialisations, with senior architecture and product leadership concentrated at the San Jose campus.

## Acquisitions Filling Capability Gaps

Three transactions between fiscal 2023 and early fiscal 2024 illustrated Zscaler's approach to inorganic IP accumulation. Airgap Networks, acquired in fiscal 2023, contributed agentless segmentation technology for operational technology environments — manufacturing equipment, utilities infrastructure, and medical devices unable to run conventional endpoint agents. Canonic Security, also acquired in fiscal 2023, added SaaS application security posture management: visibility into OAuth token grants, API integrations, and third-party application risk across enterprise SaaS estates.

Avalor, acquired in February 2024 and widely reported at approximately $350 million, was the most consequential transaction. Avalor had built a security data fabric designed to ingest and normalise telemetry from heterogeneous security tooling. Zscaler used the technology as the engineering foundation for Risk360, its unified risk quantification platform. The fiscal 2024 10-K recorded intangible assets from the transaction including $28.7 million of developed technology and $95.5 million of goodwill.

## AI as the Next Defensible Layer

Through fiscal 2024 and 2025, Zscaler positioned its AI capabilities as an IP layer compounding the data advantage already embedded in platform scale. Processing more than half a trillion transactions daily provided a training corpus for threat detection models unavailable to competitors without comparable deployment density. Chaudhry stated in the [fiscal Q3 2025 earnings release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368325000078/zs-04302025_991.htm):

> "The proliferation of AI in all aspects of business is increasing the need for our AI security. We empower customers to securely adopt both public GenAI apps and their own private AI apps, and we are increasing our investments in this area."

The AI portfolio encompassed three commercial directions: AI-powered analyst workflow tools embedded across ZIA, ZPA, and ZDX; automated threat detection trained on the platform's telemetry through the ThreatLabz research function; and the AI Protect product line addressing data leakage and prompt injection risks created by enterprise adoption of third-party large language model APIs. New patent grants in the Security Operations and Digital Experience & AI Security categories — carrying numbers in the 12.4 million range — evidenced active filing activity aligned with these product directions.

The R&D framework that had emerged by fiscal 2025 combined sustained above-median investment rates, a multi-continent engineering footprint, selective acquisitions filling specific capability gaps, and a patent portfolio extending from foundational cloud proxy claims of the early 2010s through AI workload protection methodologies filed in the 2024–2025 period — seventeen years of accumulated IP anchoring the competitive position of the Zero Trust Exchange.

---

**Sources:** [Zscaler FY2024 10-K (SEC EDGAR)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368324000109/zs-20240731.htm) · [Zscaler FY2025 10-K (SEC EDGAR)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm) · [Zscaler Q3 FY2025 8-K (SEC EDGAR)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368325000078/zs-04302025_991.htm) · [Zscaler Patent Registry](https://www.zscaler.com/legal/patents)

chapters.title: Competitive intensity, billings growth normalization, FX, geopolitical, customer concentration, governance
chapters.body:
## The Risk Ledger

The same forces that elevated Zscaler to a multi-billion-dollar subscription franchise — an uncompromising cloud-native architecture, a founder who bet his career on zero trust before the phrase had currency, and an enterprise salesforce trained to displace entire network stacks — also produced a distinctive concentration of risks. As of early 2026, those risks clustered into six categories: competitive pressure from better-resourced incumbents, the arithmetic of billings growth normalization, foreign-exchange headwinds embedded in an increasingly international revenue base, geopolitical fragmentation of cybersecurity policy, elongated enterprise sales cycles, and governance concerns tied to founder ~~control~~ ==concentration==.

## Competitive Intensity

The competitive landscape Zscaler faced in 2025 was more crowded and tactically aggressive than at any point since the company's 2018 IPO. Palo Alto Networks, whose market capitalisation dwarfed Zscaler's by a factor of three to four, launched what it called a "platformization" campaign in late 2023 and pressed it hard through calendar 2024. Under the strategy, Palo Alto offered deferred billing arrangements and free transition periods to enterprise accounts willing to consolidate their security spend onto Prisma SASE and the Strata Cloud Manager. The tactic injected price uncertainty into competitive bake-offs where Zscaler had previously competed on architecture alone, and it drew direct commentary from Jay Chaudhry on earnings calls.

Cisco continued to advance a competing SASE proposition assembled from its 2020 acquisition of Umbrella (now Cisco Secure Internet Gateway) and its own SD-WAN fabric, offering procurement leverage to its enormous installed base of enterprise routing and switching customers. For a large manufacturer already running Catalyst switching and Meraki wireless, Cisco's bundled SASE pitch carried switching-cost advantages that a pure-play proxy vendor could not easily match.

Netskope, ~~still privately held as of the frozen window~~ ==whose Class A common stock had listed on Nasdaq as NTSK following its September 2025 IPO==, concentrated its competitive energy on the Security Service Edge segment where data protection, cloud access security broker, and AI workload inspection capabilities were highest-margin. Cloudflare, armed with a global network of more than 300 points of presence and a growing Zero Trust product suite spanning ZTNA, SWG, and Magic WAN, was expanding upmarket. Cloudflare's developer-native brand and competitive pricing posed a different kind of pressure — less on the largest enterprise accounts than on mid-market buyers who might have been Zscaler's next cohort of $1M-ARR customers.

| Competitor | Primary threat vector | Relative scale (approx. revenue) |
|---|---|---|
| Palo Alto Networks | Platformization discounting, Prisma SASE bundling | ~$8–9B annual revenue (FY2025) |
| Cisco | Installed-base leverage, SASE/Umbrella bundling | ~$54B annual revenue |
| Netskope | SSE/CASB specialization, enterprise DLP | ~~Private; est. ~$500M+ ARR~~ ==Public (NTSK, IPO Sept 2025); est. ~$500M+ ARR== |
| Cloudflare | Mid-market pricing, developer-led ZT expansion | ~$1.6–1.8B annual revenue |

Zscaler's structural response was platform expansion — adding ZDX for digital experience monitoring, Risk360 for unified risk quantification, and AI security workload inspection — but each new pillar also invited new point-vendor competition from emerging AI security startups.

## Billings Growth Normalization

Zscaler's revenue scaled from $673M in fiscal 2021 to $2.17B in fiscal 2024, a compound growth rate of approximately 48 percent. That trajectory made the company one of the fastest-growing enterprise software franchises of its era. The mathematical consequence of a larger base was, inevitably, a compression of percentage growth rates even as absolute revenue additions remained substantial. Investors who had priced Zscaler at peak multiples during the 2020–2021 software bull market were sensitive to any deceleration signal.

Billings — the forward-looking metric that captures contracted future revenue, including annual and multi-year agreements — carried particular analytical weight in Zscaler's reporting. When billings growth slowed or lagged revenue growth, it suggested weaker demand for multi-year commitments or a shift toward shorter contract durations, both of which complicated forward ARR visibility. Zscaler's 10-K and 10-Q filings for fiscal 2024 and 2025 disclosed the trajectory of calculated billings (revenue plus the change in deferred revenue), and the trend showed normalization from the 50–60 percent growth rates recorded in fiscal 2022 toward more moderate expansion consistent with a maturing large-cap SaaS business. The risk for shareholders was that consensus models built at prior growth rates would prove optimistic during transitional quarters.

## Foreign Exchange and International Revenue Mix

Zscaler's commercial expansion into EMEA and APAC deepened through 2024 and 2025, and international revenue represented a growing share of the consolidated total. That geographic diversification was strategically valuable — it reduced concentration in the US federal and commercial markets — but it introduced structural foreign-exchange exposure. Zscaler denominated substantially all its contracts in US dollars, meaning the company's reported revenue was not directly subject to translation losses in the conventional sense. However, dollar strength against the euro, pound, and yen raised the effective local-currency price of Zscaler's subscriptions, creating headwinds in renewal negotiations and new-logo campaigns in EMEA and Japan, where local competitors or channel-bundled alternatives could be priced more attractively.

In its fiscal 2024 10-K, Zscaler disclosed that it operated in multiple currencies and that macroeconomic conditions, including interest rate differentials and currency volatility, could affect demand in international markets. The risk was less one of translation and more one of demand elasticity: a dollar-priced platform becomes expensive in relative terms when the buyer's functional currency has depreciated.

## Geopolitical and Regulatory Fragmentation

The geopolitical environment around cybersecurity software grew more complex between 2023 and 2026. The European Union's Network and Information Security 2 (NIS2) Directive, effective from late 2024, imposed stricter incident-reporting and supply-chain security requirements on operators of essential services — requirements that created both opportunity (Zscaler's architecture aligned with the mandate) and friction (procurement committees required longer legal and technical reviews before committing to a US-headquartered cloud security vendor). Data sovereignty concerns in Germany, France, and the Nordic markets occasionally produced demands for local data residency that Zscaler's architecture accommodated through regional cloud deployments but that nonetheless added sales complexity.

In Asia-Pacific, Zscaler navigated the divergent regulatory regimes of Japan, Australia, Singapore, and India, each of which had distinct requirements for financial and telecommunications sector customers. US-China technology policy tensions, while they did not directly impair Zscaler's operations (the company had minimal revenue exposure to mainland Chinese enterprises), created uncertainty around supply-chain trust frameworks and government security approvals that affected multinational customers with operations across both jurisdictions.

## Enterprise Sales Cycle Elongation

The interest-rate tightening cycle of 2022–2023 and its residual effects on enterprise capital budgeting extended through fiscal 2024. Chief information security officers, even those persuaded of zero-trust architectures' superiority, faced procurement committees demanding multi-year TCO analyses, comparison bids, and board-level security committee approvals for transactions above defined thresholds. Zscaler's average selling price — particularly on transformational ZIA-plus-ZPA deployments that replaced legacy firewalls, VPN concentrators, and MPLS circuits — was high enough to trigger enhanced scrutiny. On the July 2024 earnings call, Chaudhry noted that deal closures remained subject to "more board-level reviews than we saw two years ago," a characterisation consistent with the macro context.

The elongation risk was asymmetric: a deal delayed was often a deal that a competitor could re-enter, and Palo Alto's platformization offers were specifically designed to exploit windows of indecision.

## Governance and Founder Concentration

Jay Chaudhry ~~held Class B shares carrying ten votes per share against one vote per share for the Class A common stock traded publicly as ZS on the Nasdaq~~ ==held approximately 26.86 million shares, or 16.8 percent, of Zscaler's single class of common stock, which trades as ZS on the Nasdaq==. As of Zscaler's most recent proxy statement preceding the frozen window, Chaudhry ~~controlled a majority of the combined voting power of the company's outstanding capital stock, giving him effective control over the election of directors, significant corporate transactions, and amendments to the certificate of incorporation~~ ==remained the single largest individual shareholder, and that stake, while well short of a controlling block, gave him outsized influence over board composition and significant corporate matters==. The [DEF 14A proxy filing](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=ZS&type=DEF+14A) disclosed the concentration explicitly as a risk factor.

~~The dual-class structure was not unusual for founder-led enterprise technology companies, and Chaudhry's record of capital allocation — the platform had reached positive free cash flow without material dilutive financing after the IPO — partially mitigated governance discount concerns. However, institutional shareholders operating under stewardship frameworks that penalised unequal voting structures reflected that discount in valuations.~~ ==Founder concentration of this magnitude was not unusual for enterprise technology companies that had IPO'd in the late 2010s, and Chaudhry's record of capital allocation — the platform had reached positive free cash flow without material dilutive financing after the IPO — partially mitigated governance concerns. Even so, institutional shareholders operating under stewardship frameworks that scrutinised concentrated insider ownership reflected some discount in valuations.== Any scenario in which Chaudhry's judgment diverged from the interests of minority shareholders — an aggressive acquisition, a pivot in go-to-market strategy, or a compensation arrangement — would have ~~limited~~ ==reduced== recourse for outside investors. That structural fact sat, quietly but durably, in every risk-factor disclosure Zscaler filed.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
At the frozen snapshot of 23 May 2026, Zscaler enters the next twelve months at an inflection its bulls have long argued was inevitable: the platform expansion beyond ZIA and ZPA into AI-workload security, data protection, and risk management that could re-accelerate billings growth from the deceleration trajectory the Street has priced in. ~~The Q3 FY2026 earnings call, delivered in late May, served as the most recent data point — revenue tracking toward a full-year FY2026 consensus of approximately $3.1 billion while management maintained an upbeat posture on the AI security pipeline.~~ ==The Q2 FY2026 earnings call in early March 2026 is the most recent reported data point at this snapshot; management's standing FY2026 guide is revenue of $3.309 billion to $3.322 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $3.99 to $4.02, with the Q3 FY2026 release scheduled for May 26, 2026 — three trading days after this snapshot.== ~~Four~~ ==Five== earnings events, one product conference of consequence, and a federal budget cycle make the next twelve months structurally legible.

## The Catalyst Calendar: ~~June 2026~~ ==May 2026== — May 2027

==**May 26, 2026 — Q3 FY2026 Earnings.** Scheduled three trading days after this snapshot, the first catalyst inside the window delivers Q3 results, an updated read on federal pipeline recovery and AI security commercial traction, and a likely refresh of the standing FY2026 guide of $3.309 billion to $3.322 billion in revenue and $3.99 to $4.02 in non-GAAP EPS. Any upward revision sets tone for the September Q4 print and the initial FY2027 guide that follows.==

**June 2026 — Zenith Live.** Zscaler's annual customer and partner conference is the primary stage for product roadmap disclosure and the ~~first~~ ==second== material event in the window. In prior years, Zenith Live was where management introduced AI security operations capabilities and signalled the expansion of Risk360 into a cross-platform risk management layer. Zenith Live 2026 — expected in the first half of June — is where the market will assess whether AI workload protection has matured from a roadmap slide into a separately priced SKU with demonstrable win rates. Any announcement of hyperscaler co-sell integrations, particularly on AWS Marketplace and the Azure commercial marketplace, would carry immediate billings read-through to Q4 FY2026 and set narrative tone for the September earnings call.

**September 2026 — Q4 FY2026 Earnings and Initial FY2027 Guidance.** The single most consequential event in the twelve-month window. With Zscaler's fiscal year ending in July, the Q4 print arrives in mid-to-late September and simultaneously delivers full fiscal 2026 results, initial non-GAAP EPS guidance for FY2027, and management's read on the federal pipeline. The Street is carrying FY2027 consensus revenue of approximately $3.63 billion against a FY2026 ~~base of roughly $3.1 billion — an implied growth rate of approximately 17 percent~~ ==guided range of $3.309 billion to $3.322 billion==. Guidance issued above $3.70 billion would represent a material positive re-rating catalyst; a figure below $3.55 billion risks multiple compression given the premium embedded in the current valuation.

**November / December 2026 — Q1 FY2027 Earnings.** The August-through-October quarter is seasonally softer on revenue but historically shows stronger billings as large annual contracts renew. Q1 FY2027 results establish whether the company entered fiscal 2027 above or below the trajectory implied by September guidance — a pattern that has historically set the direction of consensus drift for the subsequent three quarters. Any first-quarter disclosure of AI security ARR, even a qualitative range, would become a new consensus anchor.

**February / March 2027 — Q2 FY2027 Earnings.** The January quarter is a natural litmus test for enterprise deal velocity in the United States and Europe. NIS2 compliance timelines in the European Union have elevated zero-trust architecture on CISO priority stacks across the EMEA region, and acceleration in European large-deal closings would appear here before anywhere else. This call will also carry the first meaningful read on whether AI security is generating incremental ARR above standard bundle pricing or remains absorbed within ZIA and ZPA contract expansions.

**May 2027 — Q3 FY2027 Earnings.** Just inside the twelve-month window. The April quarter has historically been Zscaler's inflection period for back-half momentum, and Q3 FY2027 will establish the full-year fiscal 2027 trajectory while carrying the first signals for FY2028 expectations — giving it outsized valuation read-through relative to a straightforward quarterly beat-or-miss on revenue.

## Management Guidance as of the Snapshot

~~Following Q3 FY2026 results, management guided Q4 revenue in the range of approximately $830 million to $845 million with non-GAAP EPS of roughly $1.17 to $1.19 — implying full fiscal 2026 revenue of approximately $3.09 billion to $3.10 billion.~~ ==Following Q2 FY2026 results, management's standing FY2026 guide is revenue of $3.309 billion to $3.322 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $3.99 to $4.02; that guide is the operative reference point until the Q3 FY2026 release on May 26, 2026.== The company reiterated its platform expansion narrative on the ~~call~~ ==Q2 call==, with Chaudhry describing AI security as "both the biggest challenge and the biggest opportunity we've seen since the move to the cloud" — framing it as a net-new budget category rather than a displacement of existing ZIA and ZPA spend. That characterisation is central to the bull case: if AI security opens fresh CISO budget rather than cannibalising existing platform upsell, the deceleration embedded in consensus estimates may prove too conservative.

## Consensus Estimates and Implied Growth

The table below reflects Street consensus as of the frozen snapshot, ~~derived from analyst coverage following the Q3 FY2026 earnings release~~ ==anchored on the pre-snapshot Q2 FY2026 management guide for fiscal 2026 and on analyst FY2027 estimates carried into the May 2026 snapshot==.

| Period | Revenue (Consensus) | YoY Growth | Non-GAAP EPS | YoY Growth |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q4 FY2026 (Jul 2026) | ~$845M | ~18% | ~$1.18 | ~19% |
| FY2026 Full Year | ~~$3.10B~~ ==~$3.32B== | ~~18%~~ ==~24%== | ~~$4.20~~ ==~$4.00== | ~20% |
| Q1 FY2027 (Oct 2026) | ~$815M | ~17% | ~$1.22 | ~17% |
| Q2 FY2027 (Jan 2027) | ~$882M | ~17% | ~$1.33 | ~18% |
| Q3 FY2027 (Apr 2027) | ~$935M | ~17% | ~$1.44 | ~18% |
| FY2027 Full Year | ~$3.63B | ~~17%~~ ==~9-10%== | ~$5.10 | ~21% |

*Consensus estimates ~~derived from analyst coverage following Zscaler Q3 FY2026 results~~ ==anchored on Zscaler's Q2 FY2026 management guide and pre-snapshot analyst FY2027 estimates==; non-GAAP EPS figures reflect stock-based compensation add-back consistent with Zscaler's established reporting convention.*

The revenue deceleration embedded in this table — from 34 percent in fiscal 2024 to approximately ~~17~~ ==9 to 10== percent in fiscal 2027 — reflects multi-billion ARR scale physics, but also embeds an unresolved question: can AI security compress that deceleration curve? A company printing $3.63 billion at ~~17~~ ==9 to 10== percent growth on a subscription-software model trades on a materially different multiple than one printing 22 percent growth at the same revenue level. The spread between those two scenarios is where most of the equity return debate is concentrated.

## Metrics That Matter Each Quarter

**Calculated billings growth.** Billings at or above 20 percent year-over-year signals demand pull-through in excess of recognised revenue. Below 15 percent triggers a debate about whether deal velocity is slowing or contract duration shortening — either of which is a negative read on the forward ARR build.

**$1 million-plus ARR customer count.** Zscaler counted approximately 590 customers at or above $1 million in annual recurring revenue at the close of fiscal 2024. The rate at which this cohort expands — and the rate at which accounts graduate into $5 million-plus ranges — is the most visible proxy for platform consolidation momentum. The bull case requires this cohort growing above 20 percent annually.

**Net revenue retention rate.** NRR held above 120 percent through most of the hypergrowth period. Compression toward 115 percent or below signals competitive friction at renewal — the clearest early-warning indicator of Palo Alto Networks Prisma SASE platformisation gaining traction in the installed base.

**Federal revenue.** Zscaler's federal pipeline experienced turbulence in fiscal 2025 amid broader federal IT budget disruption. Recovery in federal ARR — which carries deal economics materially above comparable commercial accounts — is a structural swing factor across all four quarters in the window.

**AI security ARR disclosure.** Management has not yet broken out AI security as a standalone revenue line. Any first disclosure of AI security-specific ARR, even qualitatively, would become a new consensus anchor and likely drive multiple expansion if the figures are material relative to the $3.6-billion forward revenue base.

## Beat or Miss: The Goalposts

A beat against May 2026 consensus requires revenue at least two percentage points above the quarterly estimate, billings growth at or above 20 percent, and a guidance raise of at least $30 million to $50 million on the full-year outlook. An NRR print above 120 percent alongside those revenue metrics constitutes a clean positive catalyst — evidence that the installed base is upselling faster than consensus assumed.

A miss reads differently depending on the source: revenue inline but billings below 15 percent, NRR compressing to 115 percent or below, a guidance range that brackets existing consensus without upward movement, or any disclosure of a named customer departure to a competing platform. A guide-down — particularly one citing federal pipeline slippage or competitive displacement by name — carries risk of 15-to-20 percent multiple contraction given the premium valuation embedded in current price levels.

## The Bull and Bear Asymmetry

The bull case rests on platform inevitability reinforced by regulatory momentum. Zero-trust mandates in US federal executive orders and the European NIS2 framework do not compel CISOs to choose Zscaler specifically, but they force every enterprise to rationalise legacy perimeter security architecture — and the Zero Trust Exchange is the longest-tenured cloud-native infrastructure purpose-built for that rationalisation. Should AI workload protection mature from pipeline to material ARR within fiscal 2027, and should the federal segment fully recover, the bull case produces a fiscal 2027 revenue print in the $3.75-billion range against $3.63-billion consensus — which, at 15 to 18 times forward revenue on a recovering growth rate, supports meaningful equity upside from the May 2026 level.

The bear case is structurally more nuanced than a straightforward displacement scenario. Palo Alto Networks has spent three years constructing a platformisation argument — consolidating firewall, SASE, and security operations on a single Strata and Prisma stack with aggressive pricing incentives — and its installed base gives it renewal leverage in accounts where Zscaler competes as a workload add-on rather than the primary network fabric. Cloudflare's zero-trust products carry a structural cost advantage for cost-sensitive mid-market accounts. If AI security proves to be a commodity feature absorbed into hyperscaler offerings — Microsoft Security Copilot, AWS Security Hub — rather than a separately monetisable workload protection category, Zscaler's platform expansion loses its principal growth narrative for fiscal 2027 through 2029. The bear case produces a fiscal 2027 print near $3.50 billion on decelerating billings, compressing NRR, and a multiple that drifts toward 12 to 14 times forward revenue — the range where software companies with slowing top-line momentum typically settle.

At the frozen snapshot of 23 May 2026, the asymmetry tilts modestly bullish on a risk-adjusted basis. The regulatory environment is structurally constructive, the installed base generates durable subscription renewal revenue even in a softening IT spending environment, and Jay Chaudhry's track record of building and scaling four prior security companies before Zscaler suggests operational discipline that most pure-play SaaS peers cannot match. The variable is execution velocity on AI security and data protection monetisation — and that answer arrives in quarterly instalments over the next twelve months.

chapters.title: Platform expansion, AI security, federal scaling, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## Standing at the Inflection

By the time Zscaler closed fiscal 2024 with $2.17 billion in revenue — a 34 percent advance on the prior year — Jay Chaudhry had already reframed the investor narrative away from growth-rate optics and toward platform depth. The original thesis had centred on replacing legacy network-security appliances with cloud-delivered proxies; that displacement cycle was well advanced inside the Fortune 500. The next cycle, Chaudhry argued, was broader: every enterprise security workflow touching data in motion, AI traffic governance, operational-technology isolation, and board-level risk quantification represented a surface the Zero Trust Exchange could absorb. The 2026-2030 window would test whether that claim was architecture or aspiration.

## AI Security: Threat Vector and Product Category Simultaneously

No single force reshaped Zscaler's product roadmap between 2023 and 2026 more decisively than the proliferation of generative AI tools inside the enterprise. The mass adoption of ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, and hundreds of shadow AI applications created a data-movement risk that existing DLP policies had not been designed to contain. Employees submitting source code, customer records, and strategic plans to large-language-model endpoints constituted a new exfiltration surface — one that ran precisely through the inline inspection layer Zscaler had already positioned between users and the internet.

Chaudhry's framing was consistently that AI represented a structural tailwind rather than a threat to the business model. Every AI query traversing an employee's device was data in motion requiring inspection, classification, and policy enforcement — exactly the function the Zero Trust Exchange had been engineered to perform at scale. The inline proxy architecture that hardware-appliance vendors had for years characterised as a latency bottleneck was, under this reading, the only architecture capable of governing AI traffic comprehensively.

Zscaler responded with a cluster of AI-native capabilities: AI Security, a module governing which large-language-model services employees could access and what data they were permitted to submit; AI-powered policy recommendations that analysed historical traffic patterns and generated least-privilege rule suggestions; and DSPM (Data Security Posture Management) functionality extending visibility into unstructured data at rest inside cloud repositories. The commercial logic was additive — customers already paying for ZIA and ZPA were offered AI Security as an incremental module, deepening per-seat revenue without requiring a new procurement motion.

Separately, Zscaler moved toward protecting AI workloads themselves. As enterprises deployed LLM inference clusters, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, and model APIs inside hyperscaler environments, those workloads generated east-west traffic requiring segmentation, inspection, and anomaly detection. Positioning the Zero Trust Exchange as infrastructure-level AI governance — rather than merely a user-access security layer — opened conversations that had previously belonged to cloud-native application protection platform vendors, extending the company's reach into a product category where its brand had not previously registered.

## Federal Scaling: From Compliance Checkbox to Mission-Critical Architecture

The United States federal government had evolved from an early FedRAMP reference customer into one of Zscaler's most strategically significant verticals. The Office of Management and Budget's zero-trust strategy memoranda, issued from 2021 onwards, provided the policy mandate; Zscaler's FedRAMP High authorisation provided the compliance credential. Together they positioned the company to participate in agency modernisation programmes that sought to retire legacy on-premise proxy and VPN infrastructure under executive-branch cover.

Federal contract cycles are measured in years rather than quarters, and the revenue contribution — while not separately disclosed in [Zscaler SEC filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=ZS&type=10-K) — reflected multi-agency deployments that bundled ZIA, ZPA, and data-protection modules inside large enterprise license agreements. The company built the accompanying go-to-market infrastructure: cleared support personnel, dedicated federal sales engineering, and certified-reseller relationships with the large systems integrators that govern federal IT procurement. That investment differentiated Zscaler from commercial SASE competitors without equivalent compliance infrastructure and from boutique federal security vendors without comparable platform breadth.

The Department of Defense's publicly stated goal of achieving targeted zero-trust capability across its infrastructure by fiscal 2027 extended the procurement runway further. DoD's zero-trust reference architecture explicitly endorsed continuous verification, least-privilege access, and micro-segmentation — architectural principles that mapped directly onto the Zero Trust Exchange. Execution against that timeline would depend on appropriation cycles beyond Zscaler's control, but the framework alone created a multi-year federal expansion narrative that management could point to in investor conversations through the balance of the decade.

## Platform Economics and the Upsell Arc

The land-and-expand motion Zscaler had refined since the 2018 IPO followed a recognisable sequence: an enterprise entered through ZIA — replacing the Bluecoat or Symantec proxy appliance — then added ZPA to retire VPN concentrators, then ZDX for digital experience monitoring, then data-protection modules as the compliance requirement for DLP and CASB matured. Net revenue retention sustained above 120 percent throughout the company's public life reflected this compounding, with each renewal conversation carrying an expansion component layered atop the base subscription.

Risk360, the unified risk quantification dashboard introduced in the 2023-2024 product cycle, targeted a different buyer: the CISO preparing a board presentation rather than the security analyst triaging alerts. By aggregating signals from across the Zero Trust Exchange into a single risk score with financial exposure estimates, Risk360 embedded Zscaler into the CISO's governance workflow — a stickiness driver orthogonal to technical security performance and therefore resilient to competitive displacement on product benchmarks alone.

The IoT and OT security module extended the platform's reach toward factory floors, hospital networks, and utility infrastructure — environments where unmanaged devices cannot run endpoint agents and require network-level policy enforcement. Operational-technology customers in manufacturing, energy, and healthcare had historically purchased point solutions from industrial security specialists. Zscaler's entry into those procurement conversations reflected Chaudhry's conviction that the Zero Trust Exchange's inspection architecture was horizontally applicable wherever traffic needed classification and control, regardless of the underlying device type.

## Competitive Posture Heading into Consolidation

The competitive landscape entering the 2026-2030 period had narrowed around a handful of well-capitalised platforms. Palo Alto Networks — through Prisma SASE and Strata Cloud Manager, and operating at comparable enterprise scale under Nikesh Arora — represented the most direct challenger, pursuing a platform-bundling strategy that offered free or discounted modules to displace incumbent point solutions including Zscaler deployments. Netskope retained credibility in enterprise data protection ~~despite remaining private~~ ==following its September 2025 IPO and Nasdaq listing as NTSK==, with strong CASB capabilities that competed directly with Zscaler's expansion modules. Cloudflare's zero-trust product line had migrated from its developer-first origins toward enterprise accounts, offering latency-competitive ZPA alternatives at price points that pressured Zscaler's mid-market attach rate. Cisco held a large installed base through Umbrella and Catalyst SD-WAN though its cloud-security integration had historically received lower analyst assessments than the pure-play vendors.

Zscaler's structural defence rested on two compounding assets: the global PoP network through which all customer traffic was routed for inline inspection, and the telemetry accumulated across that network from hundreds of billions of daily transactions. Threat intelligence of that volume improved proportionally with customer base scale, creating a feedback loop in which larger deployment produced more accurate detection, which supported platform expansion and higher renewal rates. Smaller competitors operating at lower telemetry volumes could replicate the architecture but not the dataset — a differentiation that became more pronounced as AI-powered detection capabilities grew increasingly dependent on training-data scale.

Microsoft's continued integration of security capabilities into M365 and Azure licensing presented a distinct risk vector: not technically superior capability but procurement convenience for buyers already standardised on Microsoft contracts, reducing the urgency of a dedicated SSE purchase.

## The 2026-2030 Horizon

The structural thesis supporting Zscaler's forward trajectory rested on one durable observation: the majority of global network security spending remained locked inside legacy appliance refresh cycles that had not yet converted to cloud-delivered alternatives. Chaudhry had made this case consistently through the company's public life — that the displacement opportunity dwarfed what had already been captured — and the fiscal 2024 revenue base of $2.17 billion, set against an enterprise security market measured in the hundreds of billions, provided empirical support for the claim.

The risks were real and symmetrical. Palo Alto's bundling aggression, Microsoft's licensing gravity, and the persistent question of whether SASE consolidation would favour a pure-play or a broader security platform with zero-trust as one feature among many would determine whether Zscaler's architectural lead translated into durable market-share expansion or whether it became a premium niche inside a market that rewarded integration over specialisation.

The execution variables in Zscaler's own hands — product coherence as the platform broadened, go-to-market capacity in federal and international markets, and customer success infrastructure sufficient to sustain triple-digit net revenue retention across an increasingly complex multi-module base — were, as of the May 2026 frozen window, the principal determinants of whether the $2.17 billion fiscal 2024 baseline would scale toward the multi-billion-dollar ARR plateau Chaudhry had staked his second decade as a public-company CEO on reaching.

## Product Glossary

**ZIA — Zscaler Internet Access.** Cloud-native secure web gateway and internet access proxy. Replaces legacy on-premises firewalls, proxies, and URL-filtering appliances. Delivered as a service from Zscaler's global cloud infrastructure.

**ZPA — Zscaler Private Access.** Zero-trust network access (ZTNA) for private application connectivity. Replaces legacy VPN. Users connect to applications, not to the network; access is policy-driven and identity-aware.

**ZDX — Zscaler Digital Experience.** Digital experience monitoring layer for end-user performance visibility across applications, networks, and devices.

**Zero Trust Exchange.** Zscaler's unified platform name encompassing ZIA, ZPA, ZDX, and the expanding data protection and AI security operations portfolio.

**SASE — Secure Access Service Edge.** Market architecture category coined by Gartner combining networking (SD-WAN) and security services (SSE) delivered from the cloud.

**SSE — Security Service Edge.** The security-only subset of SASE, encompassing SWG, CASB, ZTNA, and FWaaS. Zscaler's primary competitive category.

**Risk360.** Zscaler's unified risk management and quantification dashboard, introduced as part of the AI-era platform expansion.
